    Charging on solar surplus,
    at the hour the grid is weakest

    A Fronius Symo GEN24 Plus, a Tesla Wall Connector Gen 3, a Model 3 and a Raspberry Pi 4, tied together with evcc so the car soaks up the array's midday peak on site — and holds the voltage at the feed-in point below the level at which the installation starts protecting itself.

    SC Electrica SRL Arad & Timișoara · since 1993

    The electrical installation — and the reason everything above it works. Every cable, breaker, terminal and earth in this system was put in by Electrica Arad: the photovoltaic installation, the three-phase supply to the Wall Connector, the distribution board, the protection devices and the grid connection itself.

    Thirty years in business, seventy-plus specialists, ANRE-authorised (ANRE is Romania's national energy regulator; only electricians it licenses may work on a grid connection), a Fronius partner, and better than a thousand completed installations behind them — and it shows in the part nobody photographs. Phases balanced, terminations clean, the board laid out so a stranger could read it. Software can only ever be as good as the installation underneath it. This one never gave it anything to fight, and not one hour of the work described in these pages was spent compensating for the hardware.

    If you are anywhere near Arad or Timiș and thinking about photovoltaics, an EV charger, or both — electrica-arad.ro. Ask for the full job. They are worth it.

    evcc open source · MIT

    The engine. Every control decision in this build — when to start, how many amps to pull, when a cloud has lasted long enough to stop — is evcc's. It speaks Modbus to the Fronius, BLE to the car and HTTP to the charger, it runs entirely on the local network with nothing off-site, and it supports hundreds of devices because a genuinely active community keeps adding them. It is the rare open-source project that is not merely published but alive.

    None of this was paid for. If evcc is doing this much work for you too, pay it back — a one-off contribution or a few euro a month, and the sponsor token is also what unlocks commercial charger support.

    Mihai Gafițeanu specified and commissioned the installation, configured evcc, built the Bluetooth bridge and the logger, and found the numbers that do the actual work — the 1 A floor, the 16 A ceiling, the 60-second enable delay and the 600-second disable delay. That last set is the whole system: no scheduler, no external controller, just four values chosen well enough that the car absorbs the midday peak on its own and the feed-in voltage stops climbing.

    Section 01The problem this system solves

    On a clear day the whole street exports at once. Voltage at the feed-in point climbs, and above a certain level the installation starts defending itself — by throwing away production, at precisely the hour the array makes the most of it.

    A prosumer’s case · Energy · Romania I have the right to fight. My premises, my yard, my house, my Wi‑Fi, my electricity. Romania added a third of a million rooftop prosumers and 3,789 MW of capacity in three years, on a network nobody rebuilt to carry it. The case for fixing the wires rather than the rooftops — and one household’s reasons for not waiting to find out whether anyone will.

    Why any of this exists

    One household’s reasons, in the order they actually arrived. Everything after this section is the argument they led to, and everything after that is the build.

    I had the panels first. Three years ago I chose Fronius over Huawei and the other Chinese brands deliberately, and it was not a price decision: I was not willing to hand the controls of my own generation to a state that behaves like an adversary rather than a partner. An Austrian company, European engineering, inside the European Union. It cost more. I would choose it again.

    Then I had the overvoltage problem — the one the six sections below are about, arriving at my own feed-in point rather than in a regulator’s consultation document.

    And I have a thought I cannot argue myself out of: that 2026 turns into another 1979. So I did the arithmetic instead of worrying about it. A new Tesla Model 3, charged on as much of my own surplus as I can get into it, costs less to run over its life than a ten-year-old 2.0-litre diesel — not because the car is cheap, but because the fuel is already on the roof and it is already paid for.

    So I bought the car, installed evcc, and everything else followed from that one step. Configuring evcc made it plain that I could not make an informed decision about any of it without knowing the numbers, so the InfluxDB integration went in next. Then the Grafana integration, and the dashboard began. And once there were software packages running on a Pi in my own house, the update mechanism had to exist too.

    That chain — panels, overvoltage, a feeling about the decade, a car, then everything the car dragged in behind it — is the entire project. The seventeen numbered sections after this one are what it turned into.

    253 V

    2026, and 1979

    The thought in the paragraph above, set out properly. August 2026, on one page.

    The 2026 Iran war produced the same script as 1973: a Middle East conflict severing oil supply. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which carries roughly a fifth of world oil trade — caused what the IEA called the largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market, with panic buying, fuel shortages across import-dependent Asia, and fertiliser and food-security effects rippling out behind it. That is 1973, almost line for line.

    It is not a rerun yet, and the reason is that the safeguards built because of 1973 did their job. Strategic petroleum reserves, IEA coordination, diversified non-Gulf supply from the United States, Brazil and Guyana, far lower oil intensity per unit of GDP, renewables, and the gas diversification forced through after 2022. Brent sits near $84 — painful, and nowhere near the 1980 peak of roughly $137 in today’s money — and prices are easing.

    2026 is 1973 with shock absorbers. The danger is not this shock. It is the sequel.

    What we are in is an intermission rather than an ending. Nothing fundamental is resolved — not the nuclear programme, not sanctions, not the proxies, not Israel’s freedom of action — and a tactical ceasefire is not a strategic accommodation. The years 1974 to 1978 looked like this too: an unstable pause before the second shock, which arrived in 1979 out of a revolution inside Iran. Given a decapitated leadership and a battered economy, that rhyme is uncomfortably close. My problem is not necessarily the price of fuel, it is the scarcity. I do not want to spend my precious time queuing for thirty litres of diesel; images from Russian fuel stations are not so far from becoming a reality everywhere on the globe.

    The trap underneath all of it is inflation. The 1970s became stagflation at the moment inflation expectations came unanchored, and the warning lights are on: five-year breakevens have moved from 2.4% to 2.6%, core inflation was already a full point above the Fed’s target before the shock landed, and rate-cut expectations have flipped into a hawkish hiking narrative as central banks try not to repeat the “transitory” misjudgement of 2022. But rate rises do not create oil. Containing a supply shock with them could require recession-inducing levels — which was the 1980–82 error. Policymakers are steering between both of the decade’s mistakes at once.

    And there is one ingredient the 1970s did not have. While energy pushes prices up, AI is pushing labour down. AI became the single most-cited reason for job cuts in the United States in 2026 — more than 101,000 AI-linked layoffs by mid-year, exceeding 2024 and 2025 combined — with tech-sector unemployment at 5.8%, its highest since the dot-com bust, even while headline unemployment holds near 3.8–4.4%.

    We are looking now at a world with depleted reserves, spent fiscal space and accumulated inflation psychology — which is precisely how 1979 outdid 1973, not through a bigger physical disruption (only about 4% of supply), but through a more fragile and more frightened system receiving it. This time the system carries a second stressor the 1970s never had.

    IEA on the scale of the disruption; Brent and 1980-peak comparisons in constant dollars; US five-year breakevens and core inflation against target; Challenger job-cut reporting on AI-linked layoffs and tech-sector unemployment; consensus GDP forecasts for 2026. Figures as at August 2026.

    253 V

    The prosumer build-out

    Romania asked households to put solar on their roofs, and in under three years a third of a million of them did. The wires underneath were not rebuilt to carry it.

    The state's invitation was explicit and it worked. Registered prosumers — households and small businesses that both draw from the grid and export to it — went from roughly a hundred thousand at the end of 2023 to 332,684 at the end of April 2026, and the rate has not slowed: more than 10,600 new connections in that single month, the fastest-growing prosumer population in Europe. Almost a third of them now have batteries as well.

    Registered prosumers and installed capacity (ANRE)

    October 2024~160,0002,000 MWapproximate
    December 2025294,0003,400 MWregister
    April 2026332,6843,789 MWregister, 30 April

    3,789 MW is the equivalent of more than five Cernavodă reactors, and it was assembled without a single tender, by families buying panels a roof at a time.

    253 V

    The subsidy, and its withdrawal

    Casa Verde Fotovoltaice was the state's own programme, and it is the reason a hundred thousand of these roofs exist. It was removed from the 2026 budget.

    Run by the Environment Fund Administration since 2019, the scheme offered households a non-refundable grant of up to 20,000 lei — roughly €4,000 — toward a complete rooftop system. With the grant, an installation paid for itself in under two years rather than five or six. That is the whole mechanism, and on paper it is a good one.

    The execution was less good. In its early years the AFM held installations up for two full years and definitively rejected almost 9,000 applicants, most of them for reasons that were the agency's own. Later sessions ran on a fixed budget, a limited number of places and a window that closed within hours, on a platform that fell over while it was open. Applicants kept coming anyway. Something over 100,000 households got their panels through the scheme; several times that number stopped waiting and paid in full themselves.

    Then the programme was dropped from the AFM's 2026 budget, its €286 million redirected, with roughly €76 million left behind for battery storage. The invitation was withdrawn. The installed base it created did not go anywhere.

    253 V

    Overvoltage, and who is asked to absorb it

    The regulator's own account of the problem points at the network. The remedy on the table points at the rooftops.

    When a street exports at once, voltage at each feed-in point rises, and above a threshold every inverter on it begins to curtail and then disconnect. ANRE does not dispute where that comes from: the overvoltage that shuts inverters down is attributed to ageing and undersized networks, badly set transformers, and a grid that was never adapted to two-way flow. The consequence, however, lands on the prosumer, who is disconnected — in some places several times a day — and warned against touching the inverter's settings.

    The remedy most often proposed is not a better and smarter grid. It is a legal right for distributors to reach into privately owned inverters and switch them off remotely, as a grid-balancing tool, alongside the idea of capping household connections at 5 kW. Equipment bought, installed and paid for by the household, with the off-switch held elsewhere.

    Where this document joins the argument

    253 V is the number the second half of this page is built around. It is the level at which the inverter described in section 01 curtails and stops, and every design decision from section 01 onward exists to keep the feed-in point below it without anyone being disconnected. The argument and the build are about the same four volts.

    253 V

    The Spanish blackout

    April 2025 was the case that was supposed to settle the question. It settled it the other way.

    When the Iberian peninsula went dark, the first explanation offered nearly everywhere was solar. The investigations found otherwise: renewables played no role in causing the blackout. The failures identified were a voltage miscalculation by the grid operator and conventional plants that did not perform the voltage-control duty they were there to perform. Solar generation was part of how supply was restored.

    Blame the panels, investigate, find the fault in the wires.

    253 V

    The Dutch response

    The Netherlands reached this wall first, with a worse version of the same problem, and answered it by expanding the network rather than by reaching into anyone's equipment.

    A third of Dutch homes have panels — the European record — on a grid designed around a handful of large gas plants. The response was a National Grid Congestion Action Plan: change the law so that grid-expansion permits are granted faster, secure land for network extensions in advance, and declare those extensions of important social interest so that licensing takes a year and a half less. Behind it sits network investment heading toward €8 bn a year.

    The principle is the part worth importing. The network was adapted to what the customers had already installed, rather than the other way round.

    253 V

    What the argument asks for

    One concession first, because it is a real one, and then the request that follows from everything above.

    The concession: under the settlement rules as they stand, some of the cost of all this genuinely does land on neighbours who have no panels. That is a fair objection and it deserves a fair answer rather than a dismissal. Nobody should be asked to subsidise someone else's sunshine.

    What we truly need is a Romanian equivalent of the Dutch action plan: a published programme of network reinforcement with dates attached and consequences for distributors that miss them. That does not require anyone's inverter to be switched off from a control room.

    Sources

    ANRE figures via Economica.net and InvesTenergy; Greenpeace Romania on the AFM programme; Digi24 on the 2026 budget; Economedia and National.ro on disconnections and inverter settings; Energy Magazine on the 5 kW proposal; BBC News on the Iberian blackout; S&P Global and AOL/Reuters on the Dutch congestion plan; Puterea on Law 160/2026.

    What follows is one house's answer to the same problem, arrived at from the other end. It does not wait for the network to be rebuilt and it does not ask a neighbour to pay for anything: it moves the largest load in the house to the hour the surplus exists, and holds the voltage at the feed-in point below the level at which the installation starts protecting itself. Sections 01 to 17 are how that was built, what it measures, and what it costs to run.

    Two devices act, and once the voltage is there, neither asks. A third acts at none of these levels, but its rating gives the dashboard a second reference line.

The dashboard draws it as a thin grey dotted line at 255 V, just above the red line at the 253 V curtailment point, so both are visible on one chart.

    Three thresholds, four volts apart, and only the top one opens the circuit.

    Before this build, the feed-in point regularly passed 253 V around 13:00 — the street goes on rising after this inverter has taken itself off it. Every one of those excursions was production lost for good. The DigiTOP was installed together with the Wall Connector and was first set at 253 V, then at 255 V. The relay opened at least ten times a day and took the house with it. 257 V is the current setting, found by trial and error, and the voltage has not passed 255 V since.

    The lever

    Voltage at the feed-in point rises with exported power. Anything consumed on site never reaches the street, so local consumption at midday pulls the voltage back down — and in a house like this one there is a single load big enough to matter. A battery would be the other way to absorb it; the car is the larger sink, it is on the driveway through the working day, and needs to be charged anyway. Why not for free?

    The design goal, stated plainly

    Absorb the surplus exactly when the sun is strongest. The car now takes the whole surplus and a little from the grid on top of it, and the feed-in point stays below 250 V instead of crossing 253 V. Nothing trips, and nothing is curtailed. This is not tuned for the cheapest kilowatt-hour — it is tuned for the highest local consumption during the hours the grid is weakest.

    Section 02Architecture

    Four devices, one local network, nothing external in the command path.

    In short: the inverter measures, the Pi decides, the car obeys. The charger just delivers power and reports what it sees; the car is what actually adjusts how much it draws, one amp at a time, over Bluetooth. Everything runs inside the house — no cloud account is in the loop, and the internet can be down while the car charges.

    Want to know more?Close

    Why the fine control happens on the car

    A Gen 3 Wall Connector cannot be told what current to deliver. It reports — power, per-phase current and voltage, contactor state — but the interface is read-only; the only current it modulates by itself is the share it negotiates inside a power-sharing group. All of the modulation has to be commanded on the vehicle, which is why the Bluetooth bridge is the centrepiece of the build rather than a convenience.

    Commanding the car also gets underneath the 6 A floor IEC 61851 puts on the pilot signal. At three phases and roughly 720 W per amp, 6 A means 4.3 kW of surplus before charging could begin at all; the car accepts 1 A, which drops the threshold to about 720 W. Nothing signals 1 A — the pilot still offers at least 6 A and the car draws less than it is offered. This belongs to vehicle control in general rather than to Bluetooth: the fleet API reaches the same currents.

    Bluetooth or the fleet API

    Both routes command the car. They differ in what they cost, what they depend on, and who else is in the path.

    The two control paths
    Bluetooth LE this buildFleet API
    Runs onThe Pi, over BLE, 5–15 m from the carTesla's servers, over the internet
    NeedsA paired key on the PiDeveloper account, app approval, OAuth client, access and refresh tokens
    CostsNothing$10 monthly credit, then metered
    Works when the car is awayNoYes
    Third party in the pathNoneTesla, plus a command proxy
    Why this build chose Bluetooth

    The car is on the driveway, the Pi is a few metres away, and the one thing the fleet API offers — control from anywhere — is worth nothing here. Against that it wants an account, tokens, a public command proxy, an internet connection in the command path, and a meter that ticks every time the controller changes its mind. The controller changes its mind all day.

    There is a second cost worth naming. A Tesla Wall Connector cannot control itself, so an internet-based setup needs a public command proxy to sign commands on the way through — another moving part, and a third party holding credentials to the car. The Bluetooth bridge is that proxy, running on the Pi, reachable by nobody outside the house.

    Section 03The hardware

    The inverter, the charger, the board and the car appear elsewhere in this document. These three carry everything else — the control stack and the network it runs on.

    Three small purchases carry the whole control stack: a Raspberry Pi, a memory card for its system, and an ordinary USB disk for the measurement history. Everything else in this section is advice on where to put them.

    Want to know more?Close

    The full list, before touching anything

    1. A Raspberry Pi 4 B, its original USB-C power supply, and a microSD card of 16 GB or more
    2. A USB disk for the history — any size, and an old spinning drive is fine. See the note below before you buy one
    3. A laptop with Raspberry Pi Imager installed, and WinSCP or any SCP client
    4. A Fronius GEN24 inverter on the same network, with a Smart Meter at the feed-in point read through it
    5. A Tesla Wall Connector Gen 3 and the QR-code card that shipped with it
    6. The car's NFC key card — the physical card, not the phone key
    7. The inverter's Customer password, or owner access to Fronius Solar.web to reset it
    8. A router with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and access to its admin page for DHCP reservations
    9. An Ethernet cable from the Pi to the router — the Pi runs wired; see section 07
    10. A Wi-Fi range extender, if the inverter or Wall Connector sits beyond reliable 2.4 GHz coverage
    Distance matters

    The Pi has to sit within Bluetooth range of the car — realistically 5–15 m, through no more than one wall. Next to the router is ideal if the router is already near the car.

    Why the history does not live on the card

    InfluxDB keeps every point for ever — that is RETENTION=0 in section 13, and it is deliberate, because the whole argument in section 01 is about what the voltage did over months rather than this afternoon. The voltage logger writes three points every 15 seconds, and InfluxDB rewrites its own files behind that. A microSD card is a device with a finite number of writes and no wear-levelling worth the name, and this is the one workload in the build that will find that limit.

    So InfluxDB’s two volumes go on a USB disk and nothing else does. An old 2.5” or 3.5” drive you already own is the right answer here — the database is a few gigabytes a year and it is written in a steady trickle, so neither capacity nor speed is the constraint. Two things about old drives are worth knowing before you plug one in: a 3.5” drive needs its own mains power supply and must not be run off the Pi’s USB ports, and a bus-powered 2.5” drive on a Pi 4 is at the edge of what the port can deliver — if the Pi reboots when the drive spins up, that is why, and a powered hub fixes it.

    Everything else stays on the card: Docker’s images, Grafana’s own volume, evcc’s database, every file in section 17. Grafana writes to its volume when you change a board, not once a second, and moving it would put the dashboard behind a disk that may be asleep for no gain at all.

    Put it in a black port, not a blue one. SuperSpeed USB radiates broadband noise straight across 2.4 GHz — Intel documented it in 2012 and every USB 3 enclosure since has done it to some degree. On most machines that is a curiosity. Here it is the band the Pi talks to the car on, and a drive lying on the board with an unshielded cable is close to the worst case for it. The USB 2 ports give 480 Mbit/s, which is hundreds of times more than two loggers writing a handful of points every 15 seconds will ever ask for, so the trade costs you nothing at all. The installer’s storage step reads the link speed back and says so if the disk ended up on a blue one. Route the cable away from the board while you are there, and see section 10 if pairing is already misbehaving.

    Measured, on the disk this build uses. A 500 GB USB drive in a Gembird 2.5” USB 3.0 enclosure — the kind that has been in a drawer for a decade. The kernel reports it as 465.8 GiB, and after one ext4 partition with the root reserve dropped it offers 491.1 GB usable. Keeping the default 5% reserve would have set aside about 24.6 GB for a root filesystem that will never live there. At the rate the two loggers write, capacity is not the number that will ever run out on this disk.

    The build, in order

    Sections 04 to 11 are the sequence, and it is sorted by what each step needs rather than by where the work ends up. The two devices configured through a browser come first: the inverter is a web form and the Wall Connector a phone app, both done from the Windows laptop you are reading this on, with no Pi in the building and every check answered from that laptop. The board and the addressing follow, because both are settled before anything is plugged in. Then the card and the installer, by which time the two interfaces the installer probes are already answering. Only the car is left after it, because pairing needs a key card and a driver’s seat. Each section carries the check that proves it rather than the appearance that suggests it.

    Section 04The inverter

    Two interfaces to switch on: Modbus for evcc, the Solar API for the voltage readings that feed the dashboard. Both are a web form in the inverter, reached from a browser on the home network, so this is done before the Pi is built rather than after — and the installer, when it runs, finds them already answering.

    The inverter has two switches to flip in its own web page — one lets the Pi read the meters, the other exposes the voltages. Five minutes in a browser, done before the Pi even exists.

    Want to know more?Close

    If you do not have the Customer password

    No installer is needed. The registered system owner in Solar.web can reset it:

    1. Tap the optical sensor on the front of the inverter once — the right-hand LED flashes blue and the WLAN access point opens
    2. Open the inverter's web interface in a browser, from the home network, at its usual address
    3. Click Forgot password? for the Customer role — a PIN is generated
    4. Go to Fronius Solar.web → Settings → Components → Actions on the inverter → Reset Customer Password
    5. Enter the PIN, take the recovery key, set the new password
    Owner only

    The function only appears to the account registered as owner of the system in Solar.web. The Technician password — the role that holds the 253 V over-voltage setting — can be reset solely through the installer or Fronius support.

    Modbus TCP — the data source for evcc

    In the inverter's interface: Communication → Modbus.

    Modbus TCP settings
    SettingValue
    Slave as Modbus TCPenabled
    Port502
    SunSpec model typeint + SF
    Meter address200

    Save. The inverter may briefly report a stopped state — it is restarting its communication side and comes back on its own within a minute or two.

    Two SunSpec units on one address

    The inverter is always unit 1; the Smart Meter is unit 200. Both are reached at the same IP and port. That distinction is what lets one device serve as both the solar meter and the grid meter in section 11 — and getting it right is the difference between a measured PV figure and a derived one.

    Solar API — the voltage source for the logger

    Communication → Solar API → enabled. It coexists with Modbus without issue. Nothing here can be tested yet: both switches are proved from the Pi, which does not exist at this point in the build. Section 09 runs those two checks as soon as there is a shell to run them from.

    Section 05The Wall Connector

    All it has to do is join the network; everything else is read locally.

    The charger only needs to join the home Wi-Fi, from the Tesla app, standing next to it. After that it is never configured again — it just reports what it sees.

    Want to know more?Close

    From the Tesla app: profile → Add product → Wall Connector, then scan the QR code from the quickstart card or the label on the side of the unit. The app connects over Bluetooth, so stand near the charger, then join it to the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. Once connected, find it in the router's client list and reserve whatever address it picked up. The installer never asks for it and never records it — the Wall Connector belongs to evcc, and you enter this address once in evcc's browser configuration in section 11. Reserve it first so that what you type there stays true.

    Three numbers not to misread

    grid_v is not a second opinion on the inverter. This charger reported 225.2 V within a minute of the Solar API reporting 240.4 V on L1 — fifteen volts apart, with the contactor open and no current flowing anywhere. Voltage drop needs load, and there was none, so that gap is not the cable: it is two devices measuring to different standards, and the Wall Connector’s is the coarser. Nothing reads it. evcc regulates on surplus from the Smart Meter (section 12), and the dashboard’s voltage panels come from grid-voltage-logger, which reads the Solar API. Treat the 225 as a rounding of “mains is present” and nothing more.

    The 0.3 A on every phase is not current. With contactor_closed:false nothing is connected to the car at all; that is the noise floor of the measurement, and it reads the same whether the charger has been idle for a minute or a week. The near-zero voltageA_v, voltageB_v and voltageC_v are the same story from the other side — those are measured past the open contactor.

    session_energy_wh and uptime_s outlive the Pi. 702.5 Wh and 587,301 seconds — just under seven days — on a charger that has never heard of this build. The Wall Connector keeps its own state and needs nothing from the rebuild, which is exactly why section 09’s installer never asks for its address.

    evse_state of 1 with an empty current_alerts is a charger sitting idle and healthy. That is the state to fetch this from again in section 15, after the car is paired, and watch vehicle_connected and contactor_closed turn true in that order.

    Section 06The distribution board

    An outdoor enclosure on the exterior wall, directly above the Wall Connector. Four rows, with the instruments in the bottom compartment.

    The electrician’s cabinet: where the grid, the house, the solar and the charger meet, with a protection relay that disconnects the house if the voltage climbs too far. Built by professionals; photographed here so you know what is what.

    Want to know more?Close
    Board inventory
    LabelMeaningDevice
    REȚEAGrid, incomingBusbars L1/L2/L3/N; ETITEC V T2 surge arresters, stamped 255/20
    CASĂHouseNoark, 4-pole; three single-pole Legrand breakers in the top row
    INVERTORInverterETI, 4-pole
    AUTOCar / Wall ConnectorNoark Ex9B C32, 415 V~
    GENERALMainNoark Ex9B C40, 415 V~
    —InstrumentsFronius Smart Meter (SunSpec unit 200) · DigiTOP V-PRO-3F63A True RMS
    The current ceiling is a software choice, not a wiring limit

    The car circuit is protected at C32 — 32 A per phase, which the Wall Connector reckons as 22.1 kW across three phases — and the loadpoint title records it. That figure assumes a nominal 230 V phase; this board is marked 415 V~, which is 240 V to neutral, and 240 V is the basis for the 720 W per amp used elsewhere in this document. The working band evcc is given is narrower — 1–16 A (section 12). The real physical ceiling is the C40 main, which the whole house shares.

    The DigiTOP V-PRO-3F63A relay displays L1, L2 and L3 on its own front panel and opens the house at 257 V — the top of the ladder in section 01. Its three readings are also the only voltages in the installation that nothing logs: the Fronius feeds InfluxDB through the grid-voltage logger, the Wall Connector reports its own per-phase voltage to evcc, and these three figures exist only on the front of the relay. They are used for cross-checking. The relay is a 63 A device behind a C40 main, so it never limits current — only voltage.

    Section 07Network and addressing

    A single flat subnet, three static reservations, seven ports — and one decision about radios that the rest of the build depends on.

    Everything lives on one home network. Three devices get fixed addresses on the router, the Pi runs on a cable, and the two outdoor devices stay on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.

    Want to know more?Close

    The Pi runs wired, with its Wi-Fi radio off

    On a Raspberry Pi 4, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth share one antenna. Network traffic on the Wi-Fi radio destabilises the Bluetooth link to the car, which is the one link in this system that carries commands rather than readings. So the Pi never joins Wi-Fi at all — not once, not to get started. It is wired before it is first powered on, it takes its address from a DHCP reservation, and its Wi-Fi radio is switched off for good by the installer. One wired path in and out, one radio doing one job. The installer does this itself, and refuses to do it while eth0 is still down — blocking the radio you are connected over is a long walk to the Pi.

    The Wall Connector and the inverter stay on Wi-Fi, on the router's IoT SSID — both refuse 5 GHz networks, so it has to be the 2.4 GHz band.

    The SSID is separate. The subnet is not.

    Putting the two outdoor devices on an IoT network is worth doing for tidiness, but it is not isolation. Everything still shares one flat subnet, and it has to: the Pi is wired, the inverter and the Wall Connector are wireless, and every reading in this build crosses between them — Modbus TCP and the Solar API to the inverter, HTTP to the charger.

    Isolating the IoT SSID behind its own VLAN would cut all three paths at once. It could only work with inter-VLAN routing and firewall rules permitting those specific ports back through, which is a different build from this one. A separate SSID with no VLAN behind it is a naming convention rather than a boundary — worth knowing rather than assuming otherwise.

    Addresses

    Four addresses appear as placeholders throughout this document; three of them are the reservations the lede counts. Two of the four are the installer’s questions. PI_IP it works out for itself and offers as the default — it opens a UDP socket aimed at an address off the LAN, sends nothing at all, and asks the kernel which of the Pi’s own addresses it would have used to get there — and INVERTER_IP you supply. INVERTER_IP is used twice. Before anything at all is built, site — the second of the seventeen steps — makes the two site checks with it: port 502 accepting, and the Solar API returning a phase voltage. Much later, files substitutes both answers into a single rendered file, /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger: PI_IP becomes the InfluxDB URL both loggers write their readings to, and INVERTER_IP the address the voltage logger polls.

    The other two are never typed into the installer at all. CHARGER_IP goes into evcc’s own configuration, in the browser (section 11): the installer asks only for addresses that something outside evcc needs, and evcc keeps its own devices. ROUTER_IP is not a reservation at all — it is the router’s own address, simply where you go to make those reservations in the first place. The three reserved values live in DHCP reservations on the router, not in the devices, so re-check them after any router change.

    One consequence is worth holding on to. /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger is the only file the installer renders that carries the Pi’s own LAN address; everything else on the machine that has its own configuration reaches the machine over loopback. Telegraf and the throttling collector write to localhost:8086, the version logger reads localhost:3000 and localhost:8086, and Grafana reaches InfluxDB as influxdb:8086 across the container network. The update runner and the boot report do write to the LAN address, but they take it from that same file’s INFLUX, which is why it is the one line worth knowing about. Loopback outlives every DHCP lease a LAN address does not, so a Pi that changes address costs you that line and the matching line in /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf, where the installer keeps the answer, rather than a stack that has to be re-pointed everywhere.

    Addresses and ports
    ElementAddressPortRole
    Fronius Symo GEN24INVERTER_IP502 · 80Modbus TCP (SunSpec) and Solar API
    Fronius Smart Metervia the inverterSunSpec unit 200Grid meter at the feed-in point
    Tesla Wall ConnectorCHARGER_IP80/api/1/vitals
    Raspberry PiPI_IP—Host for everything below
    evcc UI & APIPI_IP7070Control, configuration and statistics
    Tesla BLE proxyPI_IP8080Key generation, pairing, commands to the car
    InfluxDBPI_IP8086Time-series store, org home, buckets evcc and system
    GrafanaPI_IP3000Dashboards
    Router adminROUTER_IP8443Network settings
    Four of these ports are checked, not merely opened

    Four rows above are services running on the Pi itself, and those four are the ones the system watches without being asked: 7070 evcc, 3000 Grafana, 8086 InfluxDB and 8080 the BLE proxy. Telegraf asks each of them for a health endpoint every thirty seconds — /api/health, /api/health, /health and /dashboard respectively — which is what makes “the service answers” a fact separate from “the container is running”. The boot report knocks on the same four after every reboot and writes down which of them came up, which did not, and how many seconds the machine took to get there.

    The distinction matters more than it sounds. A port that accepts a connection is not a service that answers: a cold InfluxDB opens 8086 long before it can serve a query, so the boot report gates that one on /health returning 200 and takes the other three as answered as soon as the port accepts. It waits up to ten minutes for all four and then records whatever is still silent rather than waiting on for ever — a report that never lands teaches less than a report that says the stack came up degraded, and names what was missing.

    Section 08Card, image, first contact

    Everything the Pi needs in order to appear on the network is set before first boot — and none of it is a radio. Card, cable, power, one SSH session, and nothing else typed by hand.

    Put the operating system on the card with Raspberry Pi’s own tool, plug in network and power, and log in once from the laptop. No screen, no keyboard, nothing typed on the Pi itself.

    Want to know more?Close

    Start from a genuinely blank card. A card carrying an old partition table is the most common reason a fresh image refuses to boot. Open a Command Prompt as administrator on the laptop — this step assumes Windows.

    Read the disk number twice

    clean is not reversible and it does not ask. Point it at the wrong number and it wipes that drive — the laptop's own disk is in the same list. Disk numbers change between machines and between reboots, so identify the card by its size, every time, and never by a number remembered from last time.

    Command Prompt, as administratoron the laptop
    diskpart

list disk          // identify the card by its size, not its number
select disk 1      // substitute the number you just read
clean
exit
    Pass · DiskPart succeeded in cleaning the disk. Windows will then offer to format the card — dismiss it. Raspberry Pi Imager writes its own filesystem next.

    Then Raspberry Pi Imager, with the customisation wizard:

    Imager settings
    SettingValue
    DeviceRaspberry Pi 4
    Operating systemRaspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit), under “Raspberry Pi OS (other)”
    StorageThe SD card — then enter the customisation wizard
    Hostnameevcc
    LocationYour city. It sets the timezone every Grafana timestamp depends on — every point in InfluxDB is UTC, and this is what turns it back into the hour you actually charged
    User accountUsername and password, written down — the installer asks for that username
    Wi-FiLeave it blank. The Pi is wired, and the installer blocks this radio anyway — filling it in here only creates a credential to be revoked later and an antenna the Bluetooth link has to share
    SSHEnabled, with password authentication — enough on a trusted LAN; keys are the stricter option
    Raspberry Pi ConnectNot needed — everything happens on the local network

    Ethernet cable first, then power — in that order, so the Pi has a link the moment it looks for one and never spends a boot without a network. It appears in the router's client list as evcc; give it a DHCP reservation there and that address is PI_IP for the rest of this document. Then connect to it. Windows already ships an SSH client; nothing to install on the laptop.

    PowerShellon the PC
    ssh USERNAME@PI_IP

    Substitute the username set in the Imager wizard.

    The address rather than evcc.local on purpose. mDNS works until it does not — a router that does not forward it, a client that has it switched off, a second machine that once answered to the same name — and the reservation is a fact about your network that a name resolution is only a guess at. You need that address written down regardless: the installer asks for it, and it ends up in the dashboard and in both environment files.

    On the very first boot, before the reservation exists, ssh USERNAME@evcc.local will usually get you in — the hostname was set in the wizard. Use it once if you need to, then reserve the address and stop using it.

    The first connection asks a question no later one will. SSH has never seen this host, so it prints the new key’s fingerprint and waits: answer yes and it is written to known_hosts and never asked again. On a LAN you control, on a Pi you imaged an hour ago, that prompt is a formality — but it is worth knowing that it appears exactly once, because the same prompt reappearing later means the host key changed, and on this network that means the card was reimaged rather than anything sinister.

    Pass · a shell prompt on the Pi, and ip -4 -br addr shows the reserved address on eth0 and nothing on wlan0. That is the whole of the Pi's network setup: one interface, one address, no credential stored anywhere on the card.

    Section 09Install

    Two commands, one run — the disk included. Everything it needs from the network is already switched on: fetch get.py from the public releases repo, run it, answer eight questions, and everything between a bare Raspberry Pi OS and a working dashboard is done for you.

    One small script fetches the release, proves it, and builds the whole thing. The installer asks eight questions, sets up every service, and checks its own work as it goes; the history goes onto a USB disk, which it finds, adopts or prepares for you — asking before it touches anything, and stopping rather than quietly filling the card. Ten minutes, most of it downloads.

    Want to know more?Close
    Two of the three devices are already done

    Nothing in the seventeen steps needs the inverter, the Wall Connector or the car — the script installs packages, builds three container stacks, mints its own credentials, writes its own files and imports its own dashboard, all of it on the Pi over the one SSH session you already have. But its site step probes the inverter, and taking the two browser-configured devices first means that probe passes on the first run instead of printing a warning you already knew about. Only the car is left outstanding at the end.

    Nothing is copied to the Pi by hand. get.py is published as an asset on every release, so the Pi fetches the fetcher itself, over the SSH session from section 08:

    Shellon the Raspberry Pi
    curl -fsSLO https://github.com/mihai-gafiteanu/solar-surplus-releases/releases/latest/download/get.py
sudo python3 get.py

    What those two lines set in motion: get.py downloads the release’s Debian package and its sha256, verifies the hash — a mismatch is the end, not a retry — extracts the deb to a scratch tree and runs selftest.py inside it, so a release that fails its own checks never touches the system. Only then does it hand the verified deb to apt-get, which places the tree at /usr/lib/solar-surplus/ and the units beside it, and it ends by running install.py from there — which is everything below. One release in particular is sudo python3 get.py --tag vX.Y, naming any released tag.

    The disk is the installer's business now

    There is no separate disk command and no disk flag. The storage step resolves the history disk inside the same run, in this order: a disk already carrying the influxdb label — a previous life of this system — is adopted exactly as it stands, with nothing written to it; a blank, unused USB disk is offered, and preparing it happens only after you type its device path in full; no disk at all, or Enter at the offer, and the run stops. The card is not a fallback: InfluxDB keeps every point for ever and the two loggers add three of them every 15 seconds, and a card answers that workload with a wear-out rather than an error.

    The one destructive moment, and its locks

    Preparing a blank disk erases it, so it is the one act in this build behind a typed confirmation: the installer lists only disks nothing is using, and still asks you to type the device path in full — a pipe cannot answer, and Enter ends the run rather than falling back to the card. Read the listing before you type. The card this Pi runs from is mmcblk0 and is never in the list, because everything mounted is excluded; the disk you mean is the one whose size you recognise, with no filesystem and nothing mounted.

    Everything that could stop it runs before the first byte is written. It refuses a partition where a whole disk is meant, any disk with something mounted from it, a disk carrying swap, and a disk with an array or volume group on top — the first two of those rule out the card twice over, without depending on you reading a name correctly. What it leaves behind: one GPT partition, ext4, labelled influxdb with no reserved blocks, and an /etc/fstab line naming it by UUID with the options defaults,noatime,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=30,x-systemd.before=docker.service. The label is what a later reinstall adopts the disk by; the UUID is because an old drive on a different port comes back with a different name; nofail is because a Pi that stops at a maintenance shell over a sleepy disk is a Pi with no network and nothing charging.

    That is the whole of it. The script is standard-library Python — Raspberry Pi OS Lite already has python3, and an installer that needs pip before it can install anything is an installer that fails on the one machine where nothing is installed yet. maintenance-backup.py beside it — the one backup-and-restore tool, the retired backup.py and restore.py folded into it — holds to the same rule, for the same reason.

    Responsethe storage step meeting a blank disk, once
    ── The disk the history lives on ───────────────────────────────────

  No disk is mounted at /mnt/influxdb, but this Pi has a USB disk nothing is using:

      [1]  /dev/sda       465.8G Generic

  Preparing a disk ERASES everything on it — you will be asked to confirm first.
  Type 1 to prepare it, or Enter to stop without a disk: 1

── Prepare /dev/sda for InfluxDB ────────────────────────────────────
  /dev/sda — 500.1 GB Generic
    NAME   SIZE TYPE FSTYPE LABEL MOUNTPOINTS
    sda  465.8G disk

  warn    EVERYTHING ON /dev/sda WILL BE DESTROYED.
  Type the device path to confirm, or anything else to stop: /dev/sda
  ok      old signatures wiped
  ok      one GPT partition, /dev/sda1
  ok      ext4, label influxdb, no reserved blocks
  ok      UUID 63ea7203-5039-40c5-ba06-f36d695088d0
  ok      /etc/fstab written
          UUID=63ea7203-5039-40c5-ba06-f36d695088d0  /mnt/influxdb  ext4  \
          defaults,noatime,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=30,\
          x-systemd.before=docker.service  0  2
  ok      mounted at /mnt/influxdb (ext4)
  ok      491.1 GB usable

    On a reinstall the same step never reaches that prompt: the disk carries the influxdb label from its first life, so the step adopts it — an /etc/fstab line by UUID, a mount, not one byte written — and the history is simply back. The three outcomes are ranked exactly so that the destructive one comes last, cannot touch a disk in use, and cannot happen at all without a human typing at a terminal. The prompt’s own wording still offers the card; the step no longer does. Press Enter and nothing is erased and nothing is mounted, so the run stops there — naming any USB disk it left alone, and why it left it alone, because “but it is right there” is otherwise an hour of your evening — and printing the six commands that move a history already on the card onto a disk without losing it. That recipe exists because the new filesystem mounts over the mount point: everything underneath becomes invisible at that moment, still on the card, still taking up the space.

    The manufacturer’s 500 GB is the kernel’s 465.8 GiB is 491.1 GB usable once ext4 has taken its own overhead and given back the root reserve — three numbers for one disk, all of them correct, which is worth knowing before you go looking for the missing ten gigabytes. Write the UUID down or do not: it is in /etc/fstab from here on, and blkid will tell you again.

    What it asks

    Eight questions, once. Answers are written to /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf at mode 600 and reused on every later run, so a second run asks nothing. Delete a line from that file to be asked that question again — at a keyboard: an unattended converge never reads stdin, and recovers what it can from the live files instead.

    The questions, and where each answer ends up
    QuestionDefaultWhere it lands
    Login namethe user running sudoThe docker group, and the two compose paths in /etc/default/update-runner
    This Pi's addressdetectedThe loggers' InfluxDB URL in /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger
    Inverter address—/etc/default/grid-voltage-logger, and the site check
    Where the USB disk is mounted/mnt/influxdbThe two bind devices in ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml, and where the storage step mounts, adopts or prepares the disk
    Samba server, share, account and password—/etc/default/maintenance-backup — four answers naming where the nightly backup pushes its archives. Characters the credentials file cannot carry are refused here, at the keyboard, not discovered at 22:30
    A changed answer does not rewrite what the old one produced

    Answers are kept in /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf at mode 600. Delete a line and the next run asks that question again — but it does not rewrite what the old answer already produced, because the installer refuses to replace a file that differs from what it would write. Changing an address therefore means re-running with --force, or editing the file by hand. The inverter’s and the Pi’s addresses land in one file, /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger. The Samba answers land in /etc/default/maintenance-backup. The login name lands in /etc/default/update-runner, and decides where the compose files are written.

    The script generates the InfluxDB admin password and admin token, the Grafana admin and viewer passwords, the evcc admin password and the board buttons’ token, uses them, and prints none of them: the run ends by writing them all — the three bucket tokens and the Samba account you typed included — into one KeePass import file in the login's home directory.

    What it does

    The seventeen steps, in order
    StepWhat happens
    preflightRoot, a Debian-family system with systemd, the release payload complete beside install.py — it names the scripts and the dashboard model it refuses to run without — free space on /, and a route to the internet
    siteModbus on 502 and the Solar API returning a phase voltage — both switched on back in section 04, so both should answer. Neither is fatal — a failure becomes a line in the closing list rather than stopping the run
    storageThird in the run, not eighth, because it holds the one question that cannot be asked unattended: which disk to erase. It adopts a disk already labelled influxdb untouched, offers to prepare a blank one behind a typed confirmation, or stops the run — the card is not a fallback. Then it checks what it has: a real filesystem, not the card, not one a database cannot live on, recorded in /etc/fstab with nofail and an ordering before Docker so it comes back after a reboot. It warns if the disk sits on one of the blue USB 3 ports, because SuperSpeed signalling puts noise across the 2.4 GHz band the car is reached on, then creates data/ and config/ and reports the free space
    packagesjq, netcat-openbsd, curl, ca-certificates, rfkill, python3. On the June 2026 Lite image only jq was actually missing; the other five ship with it
    dockerDocker if it is missing, and your login added to the docker group. The group is real from the next login on: until you log out and back in, every docker command in the installing session fails with permission denied ... /var/run/docker.sock — a stale group list, not a broken daemon. id shows the session; id USERNAME shows the truth
    evccThe evcc apt repository and the package
    radiosBluetooth unblocked, Wi-Fi blocked once eth0 is up, and bt-unblock.service enabled so the radio survives a reboot. With eth0 down it says so and leaves Wi-Fi alone, because blocking it would end the session you are typing in
    ble~/TeslaBleHttpProxy, its compose file and the key/ directory; the container started. The Bluetooth controller is counted before that container starts, because afterwards there is nothing to count — the proxy drives hci0 over a raw socket and every host-side tool then reports no controller at all. A key/ restored from backup is detected here and named as already paired — the ceremony in section 10 belongs only to a key the car has never seen
    monitoring~/monitoring, the InfluxDB + Grafana compose file with all three generated credentials and the disk’s path substituted, any pin the owner has raised merged back into the .env beside it, both containers started and both waited for until healthy — five minutes each. It also reports which device InfluxDB’s data volume is really bound to, because a volume keeps the driver options it was created with: no re-run and no edit to the compose file moves it once it exists
    tokenA bucket-scoped InfluxDB token with read and write on evcc and nothing else. A token already in hand is proved by a real write and kept rather than replaced — minting a fresh one while the services keep running on the old is exactly the drift this guards against — and every candidate, held, found or freshly minted, has to answer HTTP 204 before it goes anywhere near a service file. Spare twins of it are then pruned from InfluxDB, but only the ones the instance lists with their values: a spare that cannot be told from the keeper is left alone and said out loud
    filesEnvironment files, and only those: the two /etc/default templates — grid-voltage-logger and update-runner, both mode 600 — rendered from the payload with this install’s answers and minted tokens. dpkg placed the code and the units; the configurator renders the configuration that code reads, and the package and the configurator never write the same path, so neither can undo the other’s work. A rewritten grid-voltage-logger env file marks its reader for a restart in the next step, because that logger takes its file in only at start; update-runner is read fresh by every run and marks nothing
    servicesevcc and the voltage logger enabled and started. One that is already running but whose environment file this run rewrote is restarted rather than left on the old values, and one that is active but not enabled is enabled — and restarted as well if this run rewrote its file, because active-but-disabled is a real state and enable --now does not restart what is already up
    maintenanceThe evening window. It renders /etc/default/maintenance-backup from the Samba answers, then enables the window’s one 22:30 timer and the boot report — the timer starts the same unit the board’s button starts, backup, ordered updates and guarded reboot as one queued run — with enable and never enable --now, because nothing in that window may fire in the middle of an install. It enables version-logger.timer with them: the version reading fires every quarter hour at ten past, on top of the boot report's first reading and the repaint every update outcome already does. The reading’s service itself stays boot-inert by construction — the deb ships no [Install] on it, so scheduled is never boot-started, and no reading races the containers into an unknown row
    evcc-noteWrites nothing. It prints where evcc is configured and the one thing the browser configuration cannot do — the InfluxDB export — so that the omission is stated rather than discovered
    grafanaThe influxdb-evcc data source, Flux against the evcc bucket, and a read-only account called viewer for whoever checks the boards without being able to change them — created if missing, and pinned back to the Viewer role on every run, so an account that drifted to Editor drifts back. The board itself is not imported here: it reads a second data source that does not exist until the pihealth step mints its read token, and importing it now would import a board with a dead half
    pihealthThe Pi’s own patient file. A system bucket kept 90 days — health data earns no more — a write token for Telegraf, proved by a real write before it is kept, and a read token for Grafana; ~/telegraf and its container, watched for fifteen seconds after it starts, because a container that cannot read its config starts, dies and is restarted, and a single poll lands on the running moment often enough to call it healthy. Then /etc/default/pi-throttled and the host service that decodes the firmware’s throttle word, which no container can reach; then the influxdb-system data source; then the one combined board imported over whatever Grafana is holding
    os-updateThe run ends with the OS current: package lists refreshed, the pending upgrades counted with a simulated run first so the number can be printed, then full-upgrade — the same verb the nightly window applies to the OS later, and the same one the version logger counts with. If a package asks for a reboot it says so and leaves the choice to you, because a reboot in the middle of a charge is not the installer’s to take
    The three rules it follows

    It never overwrites. Every file it would write is compared against what is already there. Identical is a silent pass; different is a refusal that names the path and carries on. Nothing you edited by hand is destroyed by a re-run — --force is the one flag that changes that, for the whole run.

    It is re-runnable. Every step asks whether its work is already done before doing it, so an interrupted run is fixed by running it again rather than by unpicking what it managed.

    If a container never becomes healthy. The installer waits five minutes for InfluxDB and Grafana, then stops. That message means the probe never passed — not necessarily that the container is broken, so read the state before changing anything: 
    docker ps -a --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'

docker inspect influxdb \
  --format 'state={{.State.Status}} restarts={{.RestartCount}}'

docker inspect influxdb --format 'oom={{.State.OOMKilled}}'

docker logs influxdb --tail 20
    Restarting with a climbing restart count is a crash loop, and the last log lines name the cause. Up with the probe still failing is the opposite problem — the service is fine and something between the probe and the port is not. oom=true is memory, which on a 2 GB Pi running evcc, both container stacks and Grafana is a real possibility rather than a theoretical one.

    It says what it did, without saying the secrets. No secret is printed to the terminal — a password echoed to a screen lives on in the scrollback. Every credential of the install is written instead to ~/solar-surplus-secrets-v<release>.xml, mode 600, owned by the login: a KeePass import file named for the release, one entry per credential with the URL it belongs to, because a password that exists but never reached the password manager is the same as a broken install. On a complete run that is ten entries — the six credentials it holds for this install, the three bucket tokens (read and write on evcc, Telegraf’s write on system, Grafana’s read on it) and the Samba account you typed, recorded like the rest so that nothing belonging to this install lives anywhere else. Import it, then delete both copies; /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf keeps the same values for re-runs.

    The inverter's two interfaces, checked from the Pi

    Modbus TCP and the Solar API were switched on in section 04, from a browser, before this Pi existed. These are the two checks that prove them, and they are exactly what the installer's site step performs — run them yourself once, so that a warning from the installer can be read as a fact about the inverter rather than a doubt about the script.

    Shellon the Raspberry Pi
    nc -zv INVERTER_IP 502

curl -s "http://INVERTER_IP/solar_api/v1/GetMeterRealtimeData.cgi?Scope=Device&DeviceId=0" \
  | jq '.Body.Data.Voltage_AC_Phase_1'
    Responserun from the Pi, after the installer
    Connection to INVERTER_IP 502 port [tcp/*] succeeded!
240.40000000000001
    Pass · succeeded from nc, and a number in the 230–250 band from curl — this site sits in the 240s. The trailing digits are jq printing a float exactly rather than the meter claiming precision it does not have; 240.4 is the reading. Connection refused means Modbus is off or the address belongs to another device; null means the Solar API is off. Either one sends you back to section 04 with a web form to re-open.

    Running these yourself after the installer has already reported them is not duplication. The installer’s site step probes both and prints a warning it cannot make you read; running them by hand turns that into a number you have seen. It is also the pair to run first whenever the power panels go quiet later, because they separate “the inverter stopped answering” from every other explanation in one line each.

    What it will not do

    Three things cannot be done from the Pi, and the script does not pretend otherwise. It checks the first and the third and prints whichever is still outstanding as a numbered list at the end of the run — which, in the order this document takes, is the third of them alone:

    1. Switch on Modbus TCP and the Solar API in the inverter — a web form on the inverter (section 04) done already
    2. Join the Wall Connector to Wi-Fi — the Tesla app, standing next to the charger (section 05) done already, and not checked here
    3. Generate the BLE key and pair the car — you, in the car, with the key card (section 10) still outstanding
    Flags — both of them
    FlagEffect
    --forceReplace files that exist and differ. Read what it refused first
    --only STEPRun only the named step. Repeatable — --only files --only services runs those two. For picking up after a failure, once you know which step failed
    Responsethe three steps the disk touches, gathered from one first run
    ── The disk the history lives on ─────────────────────────────────────
  ok      /mnt/influxdb is ext4, mounted from /dev/sda1
  ok      /etc/fstab mounts it at boot
  ok      /mnt/influxdb/data and /mnt/influxdb/config ready
  ok      491.1 GB free of 491.1 GB at /mnt/influxdb

── InfluxDB and Grafana ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  ok      /home/USERNAME/monitoring/docker-compose.yml written
  ok      influxdb and grafana started
  ok      InfluxDB is up
  wait    Grafana, up to 300s
  ok      Grafana is up

── InfluxDB bucket token ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ok      org home and bucket evcc found
  ok      bucket-scoped token created — read and write on evcc, nothing else
  ok      test write accepted (HTTP 204)

    Those four lines under the first heading are the whole of the disk story, checked rather than assumed: mounted, and recorded in fstab so it comes back, and carrying the two directories the compose file binds to. Nothing binds a volume to them until the monitoring step, six steps later — and Docker refuses to start a container whose bind-backed volume has no device to mount, which is what keeps a failed mount from quietly filling the card. The wait against Grafana is normal and is the one part of a first run that takes minutes rather than seconds — it is pulling the Solar Flow panel from Grafana’s catalogue, once, into a volume that keeps it.

    Pass · the run ends with five URLs — evcc on 7070, Grafana on 3000, InfluxDB on 8086, the BLE proxy’s dashboard on 8080 and the window listener’s health door on 9101 — then the path the history lives at and the one board it feeds, then the KeePass file it wrote, how many credentials are in it and the scp line for fetching it, and finally either a numbered outstanding list naming the manual steps above or the sentence saying there is nothing outstanding. The line naming /mnt/influxdb/data is the one worth reading twice on a first install. Two checks confirm the rest from the shell — systemctl is-active evcc grid-voltage-logger pi-throttled answers active three times, and systemctl list-timers shows the maintenance window waiting at 22:30 beside the quarter-hour reading — and one from the browser: Grafana holds one board, Pi health above and evcc below, with both of its data sources already selected. One thing listens on a port of its own: the window listener on 9101, whose only instruction is the board’s run-the-window press — the installer knocks on its health door before calling the run done. The machine still takes its updates in its own evening window; the button only asks for that window early.
    Measured, on a bare card — twice

    The first time, on an earlier release: fresh 64-bit Lite image, the release payload on the Pi, the installer run once, on a Raspberry Pi 4 B. Everything happened in one session with no failures and nothing typed twice: Docker installed from scratch, evcc 0.313.3 from its own repository, every container stack that release built pulled and started, the bucket token minted and proved with a real write, and the dashboard imported through Grafana’s API rather than the file fallback. The closing list held only what it should — a fresh login for the docker group, and the car.

    And measured again on 15 August 2026, as a reinstall: the same fresh card and one run, then the pairing key restored from its archive — the sequence maintenance-backup.py --restore now automates, run by hand and confirmed step by step — and the car answered the very first request. No ceremony, no key card, no driver’s seat. That night is what this release’s backup and restore verbs are built from, and it is also where evcc 0.314 was found to export no connected or charging flag at all — which is why the board derives the charging state from power, offered current and the green share rather than reading a boolean that is not there.

    Section 10Pair the car

    A key that can charge, and nothing else. The one step in this build that no script can take, because it ends with a physical card held against a centre console.

    The one step no script can do: teaching the car to trust the Pi. You send a key from your phone, hold the key card against the console, and confirm on the car’s screen. Then you back the key up — it is the one file that can never be recreated.

    Want to know more?Close

    The BLE proxy is already running — the installer started it. Open http://PI_IP:8080/dashboard and click Generate for the Charging Manager role. That role can read data and wake the car, start and stop charging, and set the amperage; it cannot unlock or drive. If the Pi were ever stolen, the key opens nothing.

    Pairing, in exactly this order

    1. Sit in the car and keep the screen on, so it cannot fall asleep mid-procedure
    2. From your phone, in the bridge dashboard under Setup Vehicle, enter the 17-character VIN and send the request
    3. Wait for the green message confirming the request was sent
    4. Within 30 seconds, hold the key card flat against the centre console, on the wireless charging area, for 2–3 seconds
    5. The car's screen asks whether to add a new key — confirm it
    6. Verify under Controls → Locks: a new key appears in the list
    Tapping the card is not enough

    The on-screen confirmation is the step that completes pairing. Nothing appears on screen until the card is tapped — do not wait for a prompt beforehand.

    When it will not pair

    The Pi has no Bluetooth, and that is normal

    The first instinct when pairing fails is to check the radio from the Pi, and the first thing the Pi says is:

    Responsewith the proxy running
    $ bluetoothctl list
No default controller available

    Nothing is wrong. The proxy drives hci0 over a raw HCI socket rather than through BlueZ — that is what the privileged in section 13 buys — and taking the adapter that way removes it from BlueZ entirely. Every host-side Bluetooth tool goes blind the moment that container starts, and stays blind until it stops. Read that message as the proxy has the radio, which is the state you want.

    It is also why the installer looks for the adapter in its ble step and nowhere else: that is the last moment in the whole run when the question can still be answered. If it reported no bluetooth controller on this Pi there, the radio really is missing — on a Pi 4 it hangs off a UART and is attached by a service of its own, so systemctl status hciuart bluetooth is where that starts, followed by rfkill list and a dtoverlay=disable-bt line in the boot configuration.

    To ask whether the car is in range at all, take the radio back for a minute. Nothing reaches the car while the proxy is stopped, so this is a deliberate borrow rather than something to leave running.

    Shellon the Raspberry Pi
    docker stop tesla-ble-http-proxy
bluetoothctl list          # the controller comes back

sudo btmgmt find           # every advertiser, with signal strength

docker start tesla-ble-http-proxy
    Two tool traps, both measured on 14 August 2026

    btmgmt and not bluetoothctl scan on, deliberately: piped or run under timeout, bluetoothctl prints SetDiscoveryFilter success and never starts discovery at all — thirty seconds of silence that reads as an empty band and is nothing of the kind. An hour of this build’s diagnosis went to that. And when you do scan, read the name lines printed under each dev_found rather than grepping the dev_found lines alone — the name is what identifies the car, and it prints on its own line. A second hour went to that.

    One more line that is not what it looks like: can’t accept: listner timed out in the proxy’s docker logs is the accept loop’s idle timer, present in perfectly healthy runs — it is not a failed pairing. The line that is a failed scan reads Vehicle is not in range.

    The car will not appear under a readable name. Tesla advertises the first sixteen hex characters of the VIN's SHA-1, wrapped in an S and a C, so work out what to look for rather than scanning the list by eye:

    Shellon the Raspberry Pi
    python3 -c "import hashlib,sys; print('S'+hashlib.sha1(sys.argv[1].encode()).hexdigest()[:16]+'C')" YOUR_VIN
    What the scan tells you
    What you seeWhat it means, and what to do
    One or two devices in a whole minute, where a phone beside the Pi sees dozensA desensitised receiver rather than an empty band. On this build that was the history disk on a SuperSpeed port — section 03 — drowning the beacon out; the count doubled the moment the disk moved to a black port. Whatever else is radiating on 2.4 GHz, remove it and scan again
    Nothing at all, for a minuteThe radio is receiving nothing whatever, which is not a range problem with one car but a problem with the adapter or its antenna. Back to rfkill list and hciuart
    Plenty of devices, no carThe radio is fine. Wake the car — the app, or open a door — and scan again. A car left alone for hours advertises sparsely, and it has to be awake for the pairing request in any case
    The car, at −90 dBm or weakerRange. Move the Pi closer, or take a wall out of the path. Section 03 puts the working distance at 5–15 m through no more than one wall
    The car, at a healthy signalNot the radio. The failure is in the pairing sequence itself: the car asleep, the 30-second window missed, the card not flat on the console, or the on-screen confirmation never accepted
    Before you blame the radio, check what else is on 2.4 GHz

    Two things in this build sit on that band by design. The Pi's Wi-Fi shares one antenna with Bluetooth, which is why section 07 blocks that radio and the installer does it for you — confirm with rfkill list that Wi-Fi is blocked and Bluetooth is not. And the USB disk from section 03 is a 2.4 GHz noise source if it is on a SuperSpeed port; the storage step says so during the run, and moving it to a USB 2 port costs nothing.

    Browserthe whole chain, with the real VIN
    http://PI_IP:8080/api/1/vehicles/YOUR_VIN/vehicle_data?endpoints=charge_state&wakeup=true
    Responseabridged
