    Pass · JSON carrying the battery state means the bridge both reads and commands the car. The first request takes a few seconds while the Bluetooth connection is established. Back up ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/key/ now — the release’s backup (maintenance-backup.py) writes it as an archive of its own, it is the one thing in this build that cannot be regenerated from the release, and section 17 is where restoring it makes a future reinstall skip this whole section.

    The same request is also the diagnostic for this whole section, because its two failures name their own causes. "Vehicle is not in range: ble: failed to scan for <VIN>: context deadline exceeded" means the beacon was never heard in the five-second scan — the radio side, so back up to the table above. "your public key has not been paired with the vehicle" is the opposite: the scan found the car, the connection opened, and the car turned the key away — the radio path is proven, and what is missing is the ceremony above, or the restored key from section 17 that makes the ceremony unnecessary.

    Section 11The evcc configuration

    Two meters, one charger, one vehicle, one loadpoint. You build all four in evcc's own web interface at http://PI_IP:7070, and evcc keeps them in /var/lib/evcc/evcc.db. The installer writes no evcc configuration at all. This section is what each setting means and what a correct result looks like — the screenshots are the dialogs you will be filling in.

    evcc is told about the four devices in its own web page — the two meters, the charger and the car. Screenshots of every dialog, filled in, are below.

    Want to know more?Close
    The browser is the only configuration here

    evcc takes its devices either from the browser, which stores them in /var/lib/evcc/evcc.db, or from /etc/evcc.yaml. The two are exclusive: a file that defines devices wins and the configuration screens go read-only. This build ships no evcc.yaml, so everything below is something you type in.

    The two meters

    Both are the same inverter on the same port; only the SunSpec unit differs. Unit 1, implicit, is the inverter itself and is the solar meter. Unit 200 is the Fronius Smart Meter at the feed-in point and is the grid meter — the number Solar mode actually steers on. Maximum AC power is the Symo's 6000 W rating.

    The solar meter is not optional

    Without a PV meter, evcc has no measured PV figure and derives one from the other two, which forces derived house load to zero — not roughly, but algebraically: substitute the derived figure into evcc's house-load sum and every term cancels. Solar mode itself keeps steering on the measured grid meter, so the control loop survives; what does not is every number the dashboard shows.

    Energy Cost Assistant must stay off

    Both Fronius dialogs carry the same warning: for active charge control to work, ECA must not be activated in Fronius Solar.web — Settings → Operating Mode → Self-Consumption. It has no bearing here in practice, since there is no battery for the inverter to manage.

    The check that matters

    A grid meter that validates but returns only a total is not proof. Per-phase registers are: they show the meter is being read as a meter rather than inferred. Everything Solar mode does depends on this number's sign being right.

    The charger

    evcc's own note in the charger dialog states the constraint the whole architecture follows from: the Wall Connector cannot be controlled directly — control is via the vehicle, and the vehicle must be selected at the loadpoint. The Gen 3 also meters itself over /api/1/vitals, which is why the loadpoint has no separate energy meter.

    The loadpoint has no energy meter, and that is deliberate

    The field exists for chargers that cannot measure themselves. Assigning the Fronius Smart Meter to it instead hands evcc the whole-house grid exchange as though it were charge power. Solar mode works out the available surplus from the grid reading and the charge reading together, so when both arrive from the same meter the calculation folds in on itself and the loadpoint is offered less current than the roof is producing. No errors and nothing turns red — the system simply charges slower than it should and exports the difference. I learned this the hard way, cross-checking.

    The loadpoint

    This is where the behaviour is decided. Default mode Solar, with custom thresholds rather than “maximum solar”:

    Loadpoint — as configured
    SettingValueWhy
    TitleTesla Wall Connector Gen 3, 22kW, Wi-Fi, Type 2, 32ARecords the hardware and the circuit rating, which the current range no longer does
    Energy meternoneThe Gen 3 meters itself
    Default modeSolarThe mode a vehicle falls into when it connects
    Enable threshold / delay0 W / 1 minStart as soon as the minimum can be met for a minute
    Disable threshold / delay0 W / 10 minLong enough that a passing cloud does not end the session
    Phases3-phaseAs wired
    Default vehicleTesla Model 3Always assume this car; auto-detection off

    The vehicle

    Type tesla-ble, pointed at the BLE proxy on the same Pi. This profile carries the working current band, but it does not overrule the other two: evcc takes the tightest of the loadpoint, charger and vehicle limits — the highest minimum and the lowest maximum. All three are 1–16 A here so that the intersection is the band that was intended, rather than one nobody chose.

    Vehicle — as configured
    SettingValueEffect
    URIhttp://127.0.0.1:8080The BLE proxy on the same Pi
    Battery capacity60 kWhPlan duration and SoC arithmetic
    Maximum number of phases3Determines the minimum surplus evcc looks for
    Minimum current1 A≈720 W — the floor Solar mode modulates down to
    Maximum current16 A≈11.5 kW — headroom; the array cannot present this much

    Checking that evcc agrees

    Once the four devices are saved, evcc should report live figures rather than nulls. Nothing in the installer checks this, because nothing in the installer configured it — this one is yours to run:

    Shellon the Raspberry Pi
    curl -s localhost:7070/api/state \
  | jq -c '{pv:.pvPower, grid:.grid.power, home:.homePower, lp:[.loadpoints[].chargePower]}'
    Pass · four numbers rather than nulls, and a pv figure that tracks the inverter.

    Section 12The charging policy

    No scheduler, no external controller. The behaviour that keeps the feed-in voltage down comes from four numbers, and every one of them is typed into evcc in the browser — the loadpoint's two delays and the vehicle's two current limits, all four from section 11. The installer asks for none of them.

    Four numbers decide everything: start charging at one amp of spare sun, never draw more than sixteen, wait a minute before starting and ten before stopping. The result, measured: over 98 % of the roof’s output used at home.

    Want to know more?Close
    The four that decide behaviour
    SettingValueWhat it buys
    Vehicle minimum current1 AHow little surplus is worth starting for
    Vehicle maximum current16 AEnough that evcc is never clipped below the surplus on offer
    Enable delay60 sStart the moment the minimum is genuinely available
    Disable delay600 sHow long a cloud is tolerated before the session ends

    In Solar mode evcc does not hold a current. It tracks the grid exchange and modulates between the minimum and the maximum, so these are not a current — they are a floor, a ceiling and two delays.

    Why a single amp is worth arguing about

    Three phases at roughly 240 V is 720 W per amp. Over a nine-hour window each amp is worth 6.48 kWh at the charger.

    Current, power, and what a nine-hour window delivers
    CurrentPowerAt the charger 10:00–19:00EfficiencySoC added 60 kWh
    1 A the floor0.72 kW6.5 kWh~58 %~6 %
    2 A1.44 kW13.0 kWh~75 %~16 %
    3 A2.16 kW19.4 kWh~81 %~26 %
    4 A2.88 kW25.9 kWh~84 %~36 %
    6 A4.32 kW38.9 kWh~87 %~56 %
    8 A ≈ peak surplus5.76 kW51.8 kWh~89 %~77 %
    Why the efficiency column is not a constant

    Two things are lost. Conversion in the onboard charger costs about 7 % of whatever passes through it. The car’s housekeeping — BMS, contactors, thermal loop, 12 V DC-DC — draws on the order of 250–300 W whenever the car is awake, at 1 A or at 8 A alike. The second term is fixed, so its share grows as the current falls:

    η(I) ≈ (720·I − 275) × 0.93 ÷ (720·I)

    That fixed draw is 4.8 % of the input at 8 A, 19 % at 2 A and 38 % at the 1 A floor. The 275 W is an estimate rather than a measurement on this car.

    The floor: 1 A

    About 720 W of surplus before a session starts, and the least the car will accept. Reaching it is why the Bluetooth bridge exists rather than settling for the 6 A pilot floor, which would demand 4.3 kW before anything happened.

    The floor does no voltage work. The voltage problem happens at solar noon on a clear day, and at solar noon the loadpoint is nowhere near its minimum. The floor engages on marginal days and in the shoulder hours — when the feed-in point is nowhere near curtailment. Moving it cannot cost the installation any voltage margin.

    The gain is front-loaded. Amortising a fixed 275 W across a doubling of input is worth +18 points from 1 to 2 A, +6 from 2 to 3 A and +3 from 3 to 4 A. Above 3 A the setting stops mattering.

    1 A is capture-optimal; 2 A is efficiency-optimal

    The choice is what to do with a weak day: take the energy at a poor conversion rate, or export it and take nothing. This installation takes the energy. Setting 2 A instead would also be defensible.

    Why the two delays are not symmetrical

    One minute to start, ten to stop. A sink whose job is to be available should start eagerly and stop reluctantly.

    They cost different things. A long disable delay costs import: riding out a cloud at the 1 A floor draws 720 W for the duration — 0.12 kWh across the full ten minutes. A long enable delay costs availability, which is worse: sun breaks are often shorter than five minutes, so a five-minute enable delay would leave the loadpoint idle through precisely the events it exists to absorb.

    The low floor is what makes the long disable delay affordable. Import is money; export is voltage. This installation is tuned for voltage, so the delays sit at 1 and 10.

    The ceiling: 16 A

    The ceiling exists so evcc is never clipped below the surplus on offer. It is not a target and it is never reached: the inverter caps at 6 kW AC, so the largest surplus this array can present is about 8.3 A — and that assumes a house drawing nothing. In practice the loadpoint spends the middle of the day between 3 and 6 A.

    Anything above 8.3 A behaves identically, so 16 A is headroom rather than a control. A ceiling set below peak surplus would not be: at 6 A the loadpoint would be held back on the best hours of the best days, and the remainder would go to the street.

    What the arrangement achieves

    A representative afternoon: 6.05 kW off the roof, 3.70 kW to the house, 2.25 kW to the car, 97 W exported — better than 98 % consumed on site.

    Phase voltage does not go above 250 V. The inverter never reaches its 253 V threshold, so no production is thrown away — and the feed-in point is not being pushed up into the neighbours' equipment either. Voltage rise on a shared feeder is a shared problem; energy consumed on site never travels far enough to become one.

    The window, without a scheduler

    evcc has no “do not start before” setting and this build does not add one. Solar mode's own arithmetic lands the session close to the intended window: charging begins when surplus exceeds the minimum and ends when it does not. In high summer sessions have started just before eight in the morning and tapered out through the evening.

    How to shift the behaviour
    You want…Change
    More voltage headroom at middayRaise the vehicle maximum current. Each amp is 720 W taken off the export.
    Fewer start/stop cycles on a broken dayRaise the disable delay further, or raise the minimum current. Do not shorten its counterpart — see the asymmetry above.
    A better conversion rate on weak daysRaise the minimum to 2 A. The floor moves from ~58 % to ~75 % efficient, at the cost of not charging at all when surplus stays under 1.44 kW.
    A guaranteed daily amountSet the vehicle's SoC limit and let the long tail of the day fill it.
    Never import while chargingLower the maximum current, and set the enable threshold below 0 W — a negative value is export, so −200 W means 200 W of genuine surplus must be there before a session starts. Raising it above 0 W does the opposite: it permits that much import. The disable threshold takes positive values only.

    Section 13The custom files

    Thirty-nine files in one directory: eleven scripts, the seventeen units that run them, five environment templates, three compose stacks, Telegraf’s configuration, the dashboard and the two-line sudoers file the board’s buttons cross. The package places all thirty-nine under /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/, with install.py and selftest.py one level above them; the installer that follows renders only configuration — never a line of code — which is why the two can never undo each other’s work. Section 17 lists where every one of them lands. Each file below is quoted with its long header comments trimmed and the installer’s substitutions left as placeholders.

    Thirty small files do the housekeeping — the loggers, the evening window that backs up, updates and reboots the machine, and the three container recipes. The package places the code, the installer writes the configuration, and none of the code contains a secret.

    Want to know more?Close
    Every file is published unredacted, and that is a design decision

    No script in this build contains a secret, which is what lets them be world-readable on the Pi and printed in full here. The shell scripts ship inside the package at mode 755 root:root, and the one Python file beside them at 644 because its unit invokes python3 by path rather than running the file — anyone may read them, only root may change them — and the secrets live in three of the four environment files under /etc/default, at mode 600, written by the installer and by nothing else. Keeping the two apart is what makes the rule enforceable rather than merely intended: a secret written into a script would be a secret in the deb, published on the releases repository, and identical on every machine that ever installed it.

    13.1 · The loggers

    /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/grid-voltage-logger.sh mode 755 reads the Smart Meter’s three phase voltages from the Solar API every 15 seconds and writes them to InfluxDB. evcc does not publish them, and they are the entire voltage half of the dashboard. It refuses to start on a missing or malformed setting, writes only when all three phases parsed and each falls between 150 and 300 V, and logs an unreachable inverter or a failed write once per streak rather than once per attempt. Two of its guards exist because neither failure looks like one: a carriage return surviving from a file edited on Windows, and curl quietly filling in http:// and port 80 for an address written without them. It is also the one long-running reader of the environment file below, so it takes a rewritten copy in only at a restart — which is why the installer restarts it on any run that rewrote that file, and only on such a run.

    /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/pi-throttled.sh mode 755 is cut from the same cloth and writes the firmware’s throttle word — under-voltage, frequency capped, throttled and soft temperature limit, each both now and since boot — into the system bucket every 30 seconds. It lives on the host rather than inside Telegraf because the 6.x kernels removed the sysfs node the container used to read: the word now answers only at the firmware mailbox, and the mailbox does not reach into a container. It still prefers a get_throttled node where one exists and falls back to vcgencmd where one does not, and a word it cannot read or cannot parse writes no point at all — no point is better than a wrong point. Its settings sit in /etc/default/pi-throttled at mode 600, one of the three files that carry a secret: the Telegraf write token, good on the system bucket and nowhere else.

    /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/version-logger.sh mode 755 records what is installed against what is released — evcc, Grafana, InfluxDB, the BLE proxy and the stack itself — plus the count of pending OS package upgrades. Installed versions are read locally: dpkg-query for evcc, the two services’ own health endpoints, the running container’s image tag for the BLE proxy, and /etc/solar-surplus/release for the stack. Released versions come from five unauthenticated GitHub calls per run, against a limit of sixty an hour. One point per component, into measurement versions.

    It is scheduled and triggered both. version-logger.timer fires it every quarter hour at ten past — the owner’s ruling, up from hourly, its release-lookup cache shortened to fifteen minutes with it so the GitHub spend stays near a third of the unauthenticated budget — so that a row on the board can never leave you wondering whether it is wrong or merely unread, and a same-evening release reaches the Latest column in minutes. The boot report starts it as its last act, once the booted stack can actually answer, and that is still the reading that matters most: taken any earlier, a probe races containers still warming up, reads unknown, and the table then lies until something repaints it. update-runner.sh runs the file again after every outcome that ends a run, so a stale row can never outlive the refusal it caused. The service itself carries no [Install] section — the timer beside it does. Scheduled is not the same as boot-started, and it is boot-started that costs the grey row.

    The file is also a library. Sourced with VERSION_LOGGER_LIB=1 it returns before doing any work and leaves parse(), state_for(), slug_for(), probe(), os_pending() and RELEASES_REPO defined. That is how the update runner answers “is this component actually behind?” with the same code that painted the table, how a component name typed one way reaches the same case arm as the same name typed another, and how the runner knows which repository to fetch the next release from — the name of that repository is written on the Pi in this one file.

    Environment file/etc/default/grid-voltage-logger · mode 600
    # ---- shared ---------------------------------------------------------
TOKEN=REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_INFLUXDB_TOKEN
INFLUX=http://PI_IP:8086
ORG=home
BUCKET=evcc

# ---- grid-voltage-logger only ---------------------------------------
INVERTER=INVERTER_IP
INTERVAL=15

# ---- version-logger only --------------------------------------------
# Version endpoints: unauthenticated, loopback — keep as localhost.
GRAFANA=http://localhost:3000
INFLUXDB_URL=http://localhost:8086

    One file, one copy of the InfluxDB token — and six units read it, not two. Both loggers take their settings here, and update-runner@.service, maintenance-backup.service, maintenance-reboot.service and maintenance-report.service all name it as an EnvironmentFile as well, because every one of them writes an outcome point and not one of them may carry a token of its own. It is the bucket-scoped token the installer minted, not the instance admin token, so the worst anything holding it can do is write to the evcc bucket. GRAFANA and INFLUXDB_URL stay on loopback because the version logger asks those two services about themselves from the same machine, and localhost outlives every DHCP lease a LAN address does not.

    13.2 · The update path

    There is one door, and it is narrow on purpose. window-agent listens on port 9101 with two routes that do one thing each — one starts the whole evening window, backup, ladder and guarded reboot, as one ordered run of maintenance-window.service; the other starts maintenance-clearlog.service, the single marker point that begins the Maintenance details view afresh without deleting a row — and it can start nothing else: the two sudoers lines behind it grant exactly those commands. The updates themselves are still systemd talking to itself. Three timers open a window every evening, one orchestrator decides the order, one runner does the work behind its gates, and every outcome is a point in InfluxDB before the owner sleeps. From a shell the same path is one command — sudo systemctl start update-runner@evcc.service — and that is the form worth reaching for the first few times, because the journal shows each gate as it is passed.

    The evening window, four acts
    WhenWhat startsAnd what it does
    22:30maintenance-window.timerThe whole window as ONE ordered run — the same maintenance-window.service the board’s Do the needful button starts, so a timed night and a pressed one are one routine to the byte. It queues the three legs below; the After= edges hold each behind the one before it
    first legmaintenance-backup.serviceOne archive per component to the Samba share, every push proved by fetching the copy back and comparing sha256. The state a bad night rolls back to is the state before any update touched anything, so the backup goes first
    second legmaintenance-update.servicemaintenance-update.sh, the ladder: six runner instances started in a fixed order, each waited on to the end
    last legmaintenance-reboot.servicemaintenance-reboot.sh, the guarded reboot — the cold-boot path rehearsed on purpose every day, rather than discovered unrehearsed after a power cut
    on bootmaintenance-report.serviceWaits up to ten minutes for evcc, Grafana, InfluxDB and the BLE proxy on 7070, 3000, 8086 and 8080, writes what answered and what did not, then takes the day's first version reading

    The times are not arbitrary. 22:30 is after civil twilight even on the year’s latest sunset, so the window can never compete with surplus charging on any day of the year; and the whole of it clears the 03:00 to 04:00 hour where the daylight-saving changes do their arithmetic. InfluxDB is gated on /health answering 200 rather than on port 8086 merely accepting, because a cold database opens its port long before it can answer, and a version probe that races that gap writes unknown into a row nothing repaints until the next trigger.

    /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/maintenance-update.sh mode 755 supplies order and nothing else. It starts update-runner@solar-surplus, then evcc, grafana, influxdb, then raspberry-pi-os, waiting for each — systemctl start on a one-shot blocks until it exits. The stack goes first, so a new release’s pins and payloads govern the rest of the night; the OS goes last, because it is the one that can want a reboot and the window ends in one anyway. A failed instance is logged and the ladder carries on: each runner writes its own outcome point, and one component’s bad night must not cost the other four theirs. The BLE proxy is deliberately not in the ladder at all — the pins note at the end of 13.4 says why.

    /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/update-runner.sh mode 755 updates one component and records what happened. It runs as root, because apt and docker do. Six component names are valid — evcc, grafana, influxdb, tesla-ble-proxy, raspberry-pi-os, and solar-surplus, the stack updating itself — and anything else exits without writing a point at all, because a mistyped unit name is a mistake, not an outcome.

    Six words, one point each, into measurement updates
    OutcomeWhat it means
    startedWritten once every gate has passed and before the first byte is fetched, so a run that hung or rebooted stops visibly here. A run that gets this far writes two points: this one, then the word it ends on
    okThe work was done, and the message names the version now installed
    currentAlready up to date, or nothing pending. The healthy no-op, not a refusal
    approvalA MAJOR update is waiting for the owner’s yes, and the message names the command that gives it
    refusedA gate held: another update already running, a version that cannot be read, or a pin only a person may move
    failedSomething the runner attempted did not work, and the message names the step it died on

    current exists because refused used to cover both “nothing to do” and “I will not do it”, and the board could not tell the healthy row from the guarded one: a perfectly quiet night read as a refusal. Splitting the two was the whole of that change, and it is why a quiet night now reads green. The four outcomes that end a run cleanly — ok, current, approval and refused — repaint the versions table before the run exits, the runner executing version-logger.sh directly rather than waiting for anything, because a refusal caused by a stale row has to cure the row that caused it, or the board and the runner disagree for ever. failed is the exception, and deliberately so: a run that died stops where it died and repaints nothing, so the row keeps whatever it said until the next trigger.

    Four gates run in order, and every one of them runs before started is written, so nothing that never began writes one:

    What a run has to get past
    GateWhat it does
    The runner’s lockflock -n on /run/lock/update-runner.lock. One update at a time, and the second one refuses at once rather than queueing behind the first
    The nameOne of the six, after the same slug_for() the versions table used, so “Raspberry Pi OS” and the unit name reach the same arm
    The re-probeThe version question is asked again, with the library the table was painted from. current records that and stops; a version that cannot be read is refused rather than upgraded blind. The OS row is exempt, because it counts pending packages instead of comparing versions and the count is only known after apt-get update
    The pinFor the compose-backed components: whether the released version is inside the pinned track, a minor or patch past it, or a MAJOR beyond it

    That last gate is the permission boundary, and it is the owner’s rule written down: update by default, ask for a major, defer nothing. A minor or a patch past the pinned track is simply taken and the pin raised to the new track in the same run — that is the standing yes. A MAJOR is the one change that can alter behaviour somebody would have to relearn, so it is the single question this stack is allowed to put to its owner: the run records approval, names the command in its own message, and stops. The answer is a unit, not a click.

    By handsystemctl, and nothing else
    sudo systemctl start update-runner@evcc.service
journalctl -u update-runner@evcc.service -f     # every gate, as it is passed

sudo systemctl start update-runner@grafana-raise.service
…the recorded yes to a major: raise the pin and take it, in one run…

    -raise is the only instruction suffix left in the system: -force retired along with the charge guard it existed to skip, and with it went the guard’s HTTP probe into evcc’s API and the setting that turned it on. The suffix is a word about the pin, not about the gates — it raises the pin to the released version’s MAJOR.MINOR track and updates in the same run, and on a component with no compose pin it is simply the plain run. It is stripped from the name before anything else looks at it, so the rest of the run sees an ordinary component. Where the raised pin is written, and why in two places, is the last note of 13.4.

    Environment file/etc/default/update-runner · mode 600
    MONITORING_DIR=/home/USERNAME/monitoring
BLE_DIR=/home/USERNAME/TeslaBleHttpProxy

    Two lines, and both absolute on purpose: the unit runs as root, whose ~ is /root and not yours. What used to sit under them has gone with the charge guard, on the owner’s arithmetic — five minutes of interrupted charging against days spent debugging a stack that had quietly skipped its updates every sunny evening. The InfluxDB token is not here either: the unit names /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger as a second EnvironmentFile, so the token stays in exactly one place on the machine. The runner then re-sources both files itself with set -a, which is what makes a run started by hand behave identically to one started by the ladder, and what lets the version logger it starts as a child inherit the same settings.

    The solar-surplus arm is the stack updating itself, and it climbs the ladder a person climbs on a fresh Pi. It downloads the get.py that shipped with the release being installed, so ladder and payload always agree; that script verifies the sha256 — a mismatch is the end, not a retry — runs the release’s own selftest.py inside the extracted tree before anything touches the system, hands the verified deb to apt-get, and runs install.py --force in the foreground where the runner’s journal can watch it. There is no second code path: the idempotent installer is the updater. dpkg replaces the running update-runner.sh in the middle of all this, which is safe because dpkg unpacks beside the file and renames over it, and this shell goes on reading the inode it already opened.

    Two locks, and they are not the same lock

    /run/lock/update-runner.lock is the runner’s own, taken with flock -n: an instance that cannot have it refuses immediately. /run/lock/maintenance.lock belongs to the window — the backup holds it while it works, the ladder waits up to thirty minutes to take it and then keeps it for the whole climb, and hands it on. The orchestrator must never touch the runner’s lock, because every instance it starts takes that one for itself and would be refused by its own parent.

    The reboot leg refuses first, before it waits on anything at all, to reboot a machine that booted less than a quarter of an hour ago — a catch-up firing moments after a boot rehearses nothing, and could cut down a backup the same catch-up had just started; there is no reason to spend an hour on the locks to refuse for a reason already known. Only then does it wait on both, up to thirty minutes each, and if either never frees it defers with a recorded reason rather than acting: a reboot in the middle of a dpkg run is how systems die. Both locks live in /run/lock rather than /tmp, because every unit that touches them runs with PrivateTmp=yes and would otherwise be locking a private directory of its own, which is no lock at all.

    13.3 · The units

    Seventeen units, and what each one is for
    UnitShape
    grid-voltage-logger.serviceLong-running. Restart=always with a 30-second gap; After= names docker and evcc so the logger does not start writing before the stack it writes into exists. Hardened, and PrivateTmp=yes is required rather than decorative — the script writes curl scratch files to fixed /tmp paths as root
    pi-throttled.serviceThe same shape for the firmware’s throttle word, which no container can reach: the 6.x kernels keep it behind the firmware mailbox. Writes to the system bucket
    version-logger.serviceOne-shot, ProtectSystem=full, ProtectHome=yes — it only reads. No [Install] of its own: version-logger.timer carries it and fires every quarter hour at ten past, so the service is scheduled without ever being boot-started
    update-runner@.serviceA template, one instance per component. No [Install] — started by the ladder or by hand. TimeoutStartSec=7200, because a full-upgrade must never be killed mid-dpkg; Nice=10 and IOSchedulingClass=idle keep apt out of the charge loop’s way; and deliberately no ProtectSystem or ProtectHome, since apt writes to /usr and /etc and both compose files live under /home
    maintenance-window.timer22:30 daily, Persistent=true, no randomised delay — the evening’s ONE schedule since v2.38, and what it starts is the same window unit the board’s button starts
    maintenance-backup.serviceOne-shot, python3 maintenance-backup.py. Ninety minutes allowed, because the history archive crosses the LAN twice — once to push it, once to fetch it back and prove it
    maintenance-update.serviceOne-shot, the ladder. After=maintenance-backup.service; five hours allowed, which is the thirty-minute lock wait plus six sequential worst cases with headroom — selftest derives the count from the ladder’s own loop, so the arithmetic can no longer age past its components
    maintenance-reboot.serviceOne-shot, the guarded reboot. After= names both the backup and the ladder; 75 minutes allowed, which is two lock waits of half an hour each plus the uptime check and the outcome point
    maintenance-report.serviceOne-shot, and the only part of the window that is boot-started rather than timed: WantedBy=multi-user.target. Ten minutes on the four ports, one point, one triggered start
    bt-unblock.serviceOne-shot rfkill unblock bluetooth, ordered Before=bluetooth.service
    maintenance-window.serviceOne-shot: the whole evening window — its script queues the backup, the ladder and the reboot in one systemctl run and the After= edges order them, the same machinery a Persistent catch-up exercises. No [Install] on the service — the timer beside it carries the enablement, and the board’s button starts the same unit through window-agent, or you do
    maintenance-clearlog.serviceOne-shot: the Clear-log press — writes the single marker point that starts the Maintenance details view afresh through the grid-voltage-logger token, deleting nothing. No [Install] and no timer: the board’s button starts it through window-agent, or you do
    window-agent.serviceLong-running, the button’s door: an unprivileged listener on 9101 whose only root paths are the two sudoers lines naming systemctl start --no-block maintenance-window.service and systemctl start maintenance-clearlog.service. Restart=on-failure, except exit 78 — a bad token or origin list stops once instead of restart-looping

    The window’s one timer carries no RandomizedDelaySec, and the absence is the design: one Pi, one owner, one fixed half-past-ten. It carries Persistent=true, which replays a fire the machine slept through at its next boot — the whole window, elapsed as one. The ordering is written down exactly once, as After= dependencies: every window — timed, pressed or replayed — queues the three legs together, maintenance-update.service is ordered after the backup, and maintenance-reboot.service after both, so it always runs in the only order that is safe; the two locks then hold whatever the ordering does not.

    Persistent=true on a reboot timer has a consequence worth saying out loud: a Pi that was off through the evening will take its missed reboot shortly after its next boot, daylight included. The script’s guards apply to the replay exactly as they apply to the evening, and one of them exists for this case alone — within the first quarter hour of a boot the only right reboot is none, because a machine that booted minutes ago has just rehearsed the very thing the reboot exists to rehearse. A long replay can still end in a guarded reboot in daylight; that is the catch-up doing its job, late.

    13.4 · The three container stacks

    Compose file~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/docker-compose.yml
    services:
  tesla-ble-http-proxy:
    image: wimaha/tesla-ble-http-proxy:2.3.0
    container_name: tesla-ble-http-proxy
    volumes:
      - /home/USERNAME/TeslaBleHttpProxy/key:/key    …written in by the installer…
      - /var/run/dbus:/var/run/dbus
    restart: always
    privileged: true
    network_mode: host
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
      - SYS_ADMIN

    The command path to the car. network_mode: host and the dbus mount give the container the Pi’s own Bluetooth adapter; privileged is what the project requires. It is the most privileged container on the machine. The two cap_add lines add nothing at runtime — privileged already grants every capability — and are written out only so this file matches the upstream README line for line, which is what makes a future divergence visible. The key/ directory beside it holds the pairing and cannot be recreated from the release.

    “Give the container the adapter” is literal, and it has a consequence worth knowing before you need it. The proxy drives hci0 over a raw HCI socket rather than through BlueZ, which takes the adapter out of BlueZ’s hands entirely — so while this container runs, bluetoothctl on the Pi reports no controller at all. That is the normal state, it is what the installer prints as it starts the container, and section 10 has the borrow-it-back sequence for the one case where you do need to look at the radio yourself.

    The key mount is an absolute path, and has to be

    Compose expands a ~ against the HOME of whoever runs docker compose — and the installer runs it as root. A ~ here would put the pairing key under root’s home: outside the login user’s home, outside the archive that section 17 makes, and gone with the card. So the installer writes the real path in at install time, and selftest.py refuses any compose file that mounts a host path through a ~.

    The mount Docker resolved is readable at any time, and worth reading once before trusting a backup: docker inspect tesla-ble-http-proxy --format '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Source}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'. The source has to be under your own home, because that is the only place the backup looks.

    Compose file~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml
    services:
  influxdb:
    image: influxdb:${INFLUXDB_PIN:-2.9}
    container_name: influxdb
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8086:8086"
    volumes:
      - influxdb-data:/var/lib/influxdb2
      - influxdb-config:/etc/influxdb2
    environment:
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_MODE=setup
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_USERNAME=admin
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_PASSWORD=…generated…
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_ORG=home
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_BUCKET=evcc
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_RETENTION=0
      - DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_ADMIN_TOKEN=…generated…
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "influx", "ping"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 30s

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana:${GRAFANA_PIN:-13.2}
    container_name: grafana
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      - GF_INSTALL_PLUGINS=lehmannch-flow-panel
      - GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=…generated…
    volumes:
      - grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana
    depends_on:
      influxdb:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  influxdb-data:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: none
      o: bind
      device: /mnt/influxdb/data      …written in by the installer…
  influxdb-config:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: none
      o: bind
      device: /mnt/influxdb/config
  grafana-data:

    InfluxDB self-initialises on first start only — organisation, bucket, admin user and admin token — so changing these afterwards has no effect on data that already exists. RETENTION=0 keeps every point forever, which is what puts these two volumes on the USB disk from section 03 and leaves grafana-data on the card. GF_INSTALL_PLUGINS pulls the Solar Flow panel from Grafana’s catalogue on first start and writes it into the grafana-data volume; the Pi needs to reach grafana.com that once, and docker logs grafana names the reason if it cannot.

    Why a named volume with a bind device, and not a plain bind mount

    The obvious way to put InfluxDB on the disk is - /mnt/influxdb/data:/var/lib/influxdb2 in the service. It works, and it fails in the worst available way. Docker creates a missing host directory for a plain bind mount, silently, without asking. So a disk that did not mount — a cable knocked out, a drive that did not spin up in time, an fstab line someone edited — gets a fresh empty /mnt/influxdb/data created on the card underneath the empty mount point, InfluxDB self-initialises into it, and everything looks fine. You find out months later, when the card is full and the history you thought you had is two databases, neither of them complete.

    A named volume with a bind device underneath behaves the other way round: Docker will not start a container whose bind device is missing — the volume is registered, but the mount that backs it fails and the container is never created. Nothing is written anywhere, and the error names the path. And the installer creates data/ and config/ only once something really is mounted — never on the bare mount point. Between them, “the disk is not mounted” and “InfluxDB will not start” become the same event, which is the only version of this you can notice on the day it happens.

    What it costs: driver_opts are read when the volume is created and never again. Changing the path in this file afterwards changes nothing at all. To move the disk, the volumes have to go and be made again — with the data copied across first, or InfluxDB self-initialises into an empty one:

    docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml down
sudo cp -a /mnt/influxdb/. /mnt/newdisk/
docker volume rm monitoring_influxdb-data monitoring_influxdb-config
# edit the two device: lines, then
docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml up -d

    The installer says this too rather than leaving it to be discovered: if the answer in /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf and the device the volume actually carries disagree, the monitoring step prints both and tells you a re-run will not reconcile them.

    Two smaller things the bind depends on

    Ownership. The installer creates data/ and config/ owned by your login, which is readable and is what a backup wants. The container does not rely on that: the InfluxDB image’s entrypoint starts as root, takes ownership of its own data directory and only then drops to the unprivileged user it runs as. That is also why the storage step refuses NFS and CIFS outright — a network filesystem is where that chown fails, and it fails after the disk looked fine.

    Ordering, and the price of nofail. A mount generated from /etc/fstab is normally part of local-fs.target, and every ordinary service is ordered after that — so the disk would be mounted before Docker started, for free. nofail takes that away. It is what stops a missing disk from ending the boot at a maintenance shell, and it buys that by making the mount merely wanted rather than required, and by dropping its ordering against local-fs.target as well. Docker is then free to start while an old drive is still spinning up, find no directory to bind, and leave InfluxDB down until somebody notices — on every cold boot, on exactly the kind of drive section 03 recommends.

    So the ordering is put back by hand, against the one unit that cares. The line --prepare-disk writes carries x-systemd.before=docker.service alongside nofail, which orders the mount ahead of Docker without making Docker depend on it: a disk that never appears still lets the boot, evcc and the car’s Bluetooth link carry on. The full options are defaults,noatime,nofail,x-systemd.device-timeout=30,x-systemd.before=docker.service, and the storage step reads them back out of /etc/fstab on every run and says so if either half is missing.

    Compose file~/telegraf/docker-compose.yml
    services:
  telegraf:
    image: telegraf:1.35
    container_name: telegraf
    restart: unless-stopped
    network_mode: host
    user: "telegraf:CHANGE_ME_DOCKER_GID"    …the docker group's numeric id…
    environment:
      - HOST_ETC=/hostfs/etc
      - HOST_PROC=/hostfs/proc
      - HOST_SYS=/hostfs/sys
      - HOST_VAR=/hostfs/var
      - HOST_RUN=/hostfs/run
      - HOST_MOUNT_PREFIX=/hostfs
    volumes:
      - ./telegraf.conf:/etc/telegraf/telegraf.conf:ro
      - /:/hostfs:ro
      - /dev:/dev:ro
      - /run/udev:/run/udev:ro
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro

    The Pi’s own vitals: processor, memory and swap, temperature, disks and disk I/O, network, the containers, and four health checks against the same ports the boot report knocks on. Everything it reads it reads read-only — the host’s / is mounted at /hostfs with the HOST_* variables pointing every collector there, and the docker socket is mounted :ro because Telegraf only ever queries it. network_mode: host is what makes eth0 and wlan0 the interfaces it measures rather than a container’s own virtual pair, and what makes localhost the address of InfluxDB and of everything it health-checks. It runs as the telegraf user plus the docker group’s numeric id, which the installer reads off the docker group and writes in: membership of that group is what lets it read the socket without running as root. Its output goes to the system bucket — ninety days rather than for ever — with a token scoped to write there and nowhere else. The two read-only peeks at /dev and /run/udev exist only so the disk collector can name devices; without them the numbers still flow, but every gather logs a warning, and a log that cries wolf every thirty seconds hides a real one.

    Every image is pinned, and two of the pins can raise themselves

    A Docker tag is a mutable pointer, not a version, so every image in this build names something narrower than latest. The two monitoring images name a MAJOR.MINOR track through a variable with a default — grafana/grafana:${GRAFANA_PIN:-13.2} and influxdb:${INFLUXDB_PIN:-2.9} — Telegraf names the 1.35 track outright, and the BLE proxy names a whole version through the same variable form — wimaha/tesla-ble-http-proxy:${BLE_PIN:-2.3.0} — because its registry publishes whole versions and no minor track at all.

    The variable form is what lets a pin move without editing a file the next release would write over. Compose resolves ${GRAFANA_PIN:-13.2} against the .env sitting beside the compose file: absent, the shipped default answers; present, the recorded word wins. So when the runner takes a minor past the track, or when a -raise instance answers a major, it writes one line into that .env — a file no release ships and no converge overwrites — and mirrors the same line into /etc/solar-surplus/pins, which rides the answers archive: the one archive a restore puts back before install.py runs. A reinstall therefore re-materialises the raised pin, instead of starting a default-pin container over data a newer one wrote.

    A raise is proved before it is recorded. docker manifest inspect has to find the registry actually serving the new track, or the run records current and says the pin waits for the first night the tag exists — a pin raised toward something that does not pull yet would fail every later night, and nothing ever lowers a recorded pin back. When the runner finally pulls, it drops GRAFANA_PIN, INFLUXDB_PIN and BLE_PIN out of its own environment first, so the .env the gate read is by construction the .env compose resolves; a stray export elsewhere could otherwise steer the tag sideways past a gate that had approved something quite different.

    The BLE proxy’s pin is exact rather than a track, because there is no 2.3 tag on Docker Hub to sit inside — the registry serves whole versions and nothing else — so every release moves the pin. That could make it the one component the runner refuses and the ladder skips, its tag moved by hand instead. It rides the evening ladder, under exactly the policy the other two follow: the window takes anything below a MAJOR and raises the pin as it goes, writing the whole new version rather than a track the registry would not serve, and a MAJOR waits for a -raise. It is still the component most likely to need attention when Tesla changes something in the car, so its release notes are worth reading when the car stops answering. Telegraf is not one of the runner’s components at all — nothing but a new release ever moves it.

    13.5 · evcc’s own configuration

    There is no file to read here, which is itself the design. evcc keeps the two meters, the charger, the vehicle and the loadpoint in /var/lib/evcc/evcc.db, written by the web interface as you fill in the dialogs in section 11. The installer does not generate it and does not read it: it describes your house rather than the software, so no release can reproduce it. What it is no longer is unprotected. The 22:30 backup archives it every night as the evcc-db family, proves the copy on the share by fetching it back, and maintenance-backup.py --restore puts it where it belongs — which is what turns a reinstall from an evening of retyping those dialogs into a run that ends with them already filled in. The pairing key under ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/key/ is the other thing this build cannot regenerate, and it rides the same nightly run as an archive of its own.

    Section 14The dashboard

    One board, two halves: how the Pi itself is bearing up and whether anything needs updating, then where the power is going and what it did all day.

    One Grafana page shows the whole system. The top half is the Pi — its vitals, what the evening window did, and one line per piece of software saying whether it is current. The bottom half is the charging: the live power flow, the day’s energy, and every trace with a time axis stacked at the foot. The installer imports it ready-made.

    Want to know more?Close

    The board is generated rather than drawn by hand, and it arrives complete. The two data sources it reads are named inside it by fixed identifier — influxdb-evcc for the charging bucket, influxdb-system for the Pi’s own — and the installer created both under exactly those identifiers earlier in the run, so there is nothing to pick from a dropdown and nothing to paste. Three things are filled in at import, and only three: the hidden constants the two maintenance buttons read — the endpoints window-agent answers on, written as the browser reaches the Pi, and the one token the installer minted with this install’s other secrets. Everything else goes to Grafana exactly as generated.

    The import is a single POST to /api/dashboards/db with overwrite set, and the overwrite is deliberate: this file is generated from the repository, so the copy Grafana happens to be holding is never the version worth protecting. The polite form was tried and cost a release — Grafana answered “already exists”, the installer counted that as success, and the previous board kept its seat on the wall with its buttons POSTing at a port that no longer answered. If the POST fails for any other reason the installer says so and writes the finished file into your home directory: Dashboards → New → Import → Upload JSON file.

    The board, top to bottom
    BandWhat it answers
    Right now
    the left zone, sixteen of the twenty-four columns    		How the Pi itself is bearing up this second: temperature, CPU, memory and both disks as gauges, with the one-minute load beside them as a figure; uptime, the age of the version reading and the age of the voltage reading; the power-supply and throttling tiles — and under them what the evening window did, which containers are up, and the update half
    Right now

    evcc

Under them one tile per phase for house voltage, charger voltage and charge current; the session row, which is what the grid is doing, the solar share now and over the session, range added and the car’s state of charge; and one full-width tile carrying the BLE proxy’s door beside the charging fact
    The window
    at the foot, full width    		Every remaining charging trace with a time axis, stacked in one column so a single moment can be read down all of it: charging state, power, energy, state of charge, voltage, and then the three phases one at a time

    The captures below are one board on one afternoon, split where it splits: the live tiles and the charging history above, everything with a time axis below. The window is 24 hours, so a full charge and the night either side of it fit on one screen.

    The pictures are of an older board

    The two stills and the recording predate the update panels’ move off the foot of the page and onto the Pi’s surface — the caption below still calls the foot of the board the update desk, which is what dates them. The arrangement they show is not the one the table above walks.

    They are kept because what they show best has not changed — the live tiles, the traces, the shared crosshair, the shape of a charging afternoon on 24 hours of axis. Read the pictures for the panels, and the text around them for the arrangement.

    Want to know more?Close

    Two things are worth knowing about the live tiles. Only they move — the whole page re-queries on the 30-second refresh, but everything below them is the whole 24-hour window, and half a minute added to the end of a day changes nothing an eye can catch. And blank is not zero: when nothing is charging the charger tiles do not fall to zero, they say not charging. The charger keeps reporting while idle — a few tenths of an amp of standby current, and between nought and three volts of residual across the three phases — so the queries are gated above that noise, at 50 V and 0.5 A, and the charger’s two tiles in a phase column fall away together. A zero would assert a reading nobody took; the voltage and the current disagreeing about whether the car is plugged in would be worse. The house voltage at the top of each column is measured at the feed-in point and never falls away — it is the one instrument in the column that is not about the car. In the capture above the car is charging on surplus alone, so all three carry volts and amps.

    The voltage panel is the one to read. Three phase traces and five reference lines — the floors at 195.5 and 207 V, the ceilings at 241.5 and 253 V, and the arrester stamp at 255 V. Four of them are 230 V nominal read as percentages: minus fifteen and minus ten below, plus five and plus ten above — and the board’s legend now names the 207 and 241.5 V pair by that same arithmetic, the 90 % floor and the 105 % ceiling — and that top one, 253 V, is also where the inverter curtails (section 04). The fifth is drawn dotted and grey because it is not a limit anyone regulates to at all — it is the arrester’s Uc marking, the voltage it can sit at continuously, and it acts at none of these levels. The system is doing its job when the traces stay under the 253 V line and nothing had to be disconnected to keep them there.

    The three House Phase tiles higher up carry the same five numbers as colour bands — green between 207 and 241.5 V, amber outside that in either direction, red below 195.5 and at 253 — so a phase is the same colour in the tile as it is a position on the trace, and the two cannot tell you different things about the same instant.

    A break in a trace is a break in the data. The logger writes every 15 seconds, and a silence longer than a minute is drawn as a gap rather than joined up across its own absence — the half hour missing after 12:30 is the Pi being rebuilt. Nothing was measured there, and the panel says so.

    Under it the same story is told one phase at a time: the current the car is drawing, against the charger’s own voltage and against the feed-in voltage. The charger always reads a few volts high, and that difference is the drop across the house wiring — which is why the regulating decision is taken on the feed-in reading and not on the charger’s (section 12).

    Every time-series panel shares one cursor, so hovering any of them puts the same marker at the same instant on all the others. It is also why nothing on this board is inside a collapsed row: a collapsed row is a panel the crosshair cannot reach, and the narrow rail of Pi traces exists precisely so that the history it carries could come out of the collapsed row it used to hide in. The charging traces keep the full width in one stack of uniform heights, and their legends are pinned to the same width, so the hour gridlines fall on a single vertical line down the block and the shared marker lands where the eye already is.

    The recording is a board rather than a picture of one, and it carries the one thing a still cannot: which parts of the page are alive. The arrangement in it is the older one again, but the thing it is counting has not changed — the refresh is still 30 seconds, and it is still the only clock on the page.

    The update half

    At the foot of the Pi’s zone the stack answers four questions in order. Vehicle SoC · now stands at its head — the same tile as the one in the session row further down the board, repeated here so the car’s charge is on the surface that is always visible. Under it, BLE proxy: the proxy’s HTTP door on the Pi, up or down. That is the owner’s ruling on prominence — it is the command path to the car, and with it down evcc can still see the car but cannot tell it to start, stop or change current, so it is the piece of software whose silence costs the most. The two of them together are “where is the car, and can it be reached” answered before anything about this Pi. The charge tile’s six rows are not free: the region is fixed at thirty-three rows by the lattice, and neither table below could give any up without growing a scrollbar, so the proxy and the panel beneath it dropped from six rows to three to pay for it. They move together on purpose — the proxy is sized against the headline it stands over, and three rows is the rail’s own trace height, so both edges still land on the lattice. Neither loses a reading by it: both say one word. Then the other two questions: am I fine, and what is each component doing. Updates — am I fine? is a single stat panel that reduces the whole stack to one word on a coloured ground. It takes the last outcome each component recorded and counts the ones that are waiting on a person; nought of them reads Up to date in green, anything from one upward reads Needs you in orange. Nought is the ordinary answer, and a healthy evening leaves the panel green and the rest of this half almost blank — which is the point of it. Before the first update has ever run it reads no update has run yet rather than a reassuring zero.

    Under it, Software versions — installed and latest is one line per component, in name order: the six the version logger reads — evcc, Grafana, InfluxDB, Raspberry Pi OS, solar-surplus itself, and tesla-ble-proxy. Installed is what is on this Pi; the OS row counts pending package upgrades instead of comparing version strings, so it reads 0 pending when there is nothing to take, in both columns — the count is its own comparison. Latest is the version each upstream reports: GitHub’s newest release, read every quarter hour; unknown means the lookup had no answer — network, or the spent hourly budget — and the runner refuses to upgrade blind on it. State is the word that component’s last update run recorded, painted as a coloured cell — with one exception that outranks the two green words: when the version logger’s own verdict says upstream is ahead of this Pi, the row reads Update available in orange until a run takes the update and repaints it. A run that ended well is not the whole truth once a newer release is published, and a green cell beside a visible version mismatch was the last run answering a question nobody asked. A third column once counted the days since a component last actually moved; the owner retired it, and the two questions left are the two the strip is for.

    The words in the State column, and what each one is
    CellWhat was recorded, and what it wants from you
    Up to date
    green    		current — the run looked, found the component already at the newest version its publisher offers, and did nothing. The healthy no-op, and what a quiet night is supposed to look like
    Updated
    green    		ok — the run installed something and it worked. Nothing to do
    Update available
    orange    		behind — the one word in this column the runner never wrote: the version logger’s verdict, painted over a green outcome — or over Not run yet — when upstream reports a newer release than what is installed. Nothing is asked of you: the evening ladder takes minor updates on its own, and a major will turn this into Needs your yes when its run looks at the pin. Pressing Do the needful takes it now instead of tonight. The words below outrank it — a run that is asking for a hand is more specific news about the same mismatch
    Running now
    blue    		started — written before the work begins, so a row still saying this long after the window closed is a run that hung or a Pi that rebooted under it
    Needs your yes
    orange    		approval — a major version is waiting. Majors are the one thing this stack asks about, because they are the one change that can alter behaviour you would have to relearn. Answer with sudo systemctl start update-runner@<component>-raise.service, which proves the new track against the registry, raises the pin and takes the update in the same run (section 13)
    Needs you
    orange    		refused — a correct outcome rather than a fault, but one only a person can settle: a version that could not be read at one end or the other, so nothing was upgraded blind; or a compose file still carrying an old literal pin, which a converge modernises. A run that arrived while another already held the lock records the same word and needs nothing from you: the next window takes it
    Failed
    red    		failed — the work started and broke. journalctl -u update-runner@<component>.service has the whole run
    Not run yet
    unpainted    		No outcome has ever been recorded for this component — a fresh install, or one whose first evening window has not come round yet. Named rather than left blank, because a blank cell reads as missing data instead of as a state. Every component is in the ladder, so the blank is temporary
    One button, and why it is only one

    Grafana’s table actions fire from the browser rather than from the Grafana server, so any button needs a listener running on the Pi and a shared token written into the dashboard itself — readable by anyone who can open the board. That is why the per-row Update buttons are gone: nine sudo-adjacent commands behind one LAN door, each pressed on whatever a stale tab happened to show, guarding decisions the nightly window was already making better on the Pi. What came back is deliberately smaller. TWO buttons, at the top of the left column, directly above the “Maintenance details” log their presses feed. Do the needful starts the whole evening window — backup, ladder, guarded reboot, one ordered run — and decides nothing from what is on screen: the press means “run tonight now”, every gate on the Pi still asks its own question when the window reaches it, and the listener refuses the press while a window is already running. Clear log, beside it, starts the details view afresh from one marker point — the history stays in the bucket, nothing deleted. Both presses confirm first, and each dialog says its consequence out loud — the reboot lands within the hour, a charging session is briefly interrupted and resumes; the cleared rows are hidden, never erased. Since v2.44 the two buttons are the board’s own HTML, six grid rows tall — Grafana pins its stock confirming button at 24 px, too small for a wall — rendered raw under the compose’s GF_PANELS_DISABLE_SANITIZE_HTML flag, with the same confirmations and the same POST behind them. The token still guards against stray LAN requests, not against people, and the sudoers lines behind the door grant exactly two commands: start the window, write the marker. The decisions still belong where the truth is, on the Pi.

    An update out of turn is therefore a unit started over SSH: sudo systemctl start update-runner@evcc.service (section 16). The runner re-probes before it acts, so starting one that has nothing to do costs an Up to date row and nothing else.

    Neither panel is bound to the time picker, and that is on purpose: what is installed on this Pi must not change because you zoomed to an hour of yesterday. The strip reads the newest point per component out of thirty days of version readings and ninety days of outcomes; the headline reads the same ninety days. The two measurements are also tagged differently — the version logger writes the display name raspberry pi os, the runner writes the slug raspberry-pi-os — so the query folds spaces to hyphens before the four streams — installed, latest, the logger’s verdict, the runner’s outcome — are stacked and pivoted into one row, or the operating system would arrive as two components that never meet.

    The freshness of all this is a panel of its own, up in the trio under the gauges. Versions last checked says how long ago the version reading last succeeded, in words rather than in hours, because “3 hours 50 minutes ago” reads as a fact where a fractional hour reads as a quantity to be compared. Green below 25 hours, amber to 48, red beyond, and an empty tile reads never, in red rather than green, because a check that has never succeeded is not an all-clear. The canonical reading rides the boot report at the end of the evening window and every update outcome repaints it on its way out, so a stale tile means the whole evening did not happen.

    Value-mapping patterns need their slashes. That tile’s value is a sentence rather than a number, so its colour comes from regex value mappings rather than from thresholds — and Grafana wraps a pattern not written in /…/ form as ^pattern$, a whole-string match. A partial regex written bare therefore matches nothing, the colour falls through to the panel’s threshold, and the tile reads red for every value of an hour or more — which is the entire normal life of a reading taken once a night.

    Section 15Verification

    The installer checks its own work as it goes. These are the three checks it cannot make for you, and they are the ones that decide whether the installation is trustworthy or merely green.

    Three checks decide whether to trust it: the numbers agree with the inverter, the grid meter’s sign is right, and everything comes back on its own after a reboot.

    Want to know more?Close

    The one that must not be skipped: cross-check every site figure

    With the car charging, sample the inverter and evcc in one command. Solar mode decides when to charge by watching grid export, so this is what proves the whole metering chain before the charging policy is trusted.

    Shellon the Raspberry Pi
    { curl -s "http://INVERTER_IP/solar_api/v1/GetPowerFlowRealtimeData.fcgi" \
    | jq -c '.Body.Data.Site|{P_PV,P_Grid,P_Load}';
  curl -s http://localhost:7070/api/state \
    | jq -c '{grid:.grid.power, pvPower, homePower, charge:[.loadpoints[].chargePower]}'; }
    Pass · PV agrees within a few per cent, grid agrees in sign, and homePower ≈ P_Load − charge.

    Meter sign

    Switch on a large load — a kettle or an oven — and watch the grid figure.

    Pass · grid import increases. If it drops, the sign is inverted and the system would charge at exactly the wrong times.

    The reboot test

    The step that proves a power cut needs no human. It exercises the After=docker.service ordering, the bt-unblock unit and the /etc/fstab line for the history disk, all for real. The disk is the reason to take this one seriously rather than assume it: a USB drive that mounts when you mount it by hand and does not mount at boot is a common enough failure, and the symptom is InfluxDB refusing to start rather than anything obviously about a disk.

    You are not the only one who runs this test. The evening window’s reboot leg takes the same path every night, and rehearsing the cold boot is the whole reason that reboot exists: a power cut is this path taken unrehearsed, and the only difference is who chose the moment. On the far side of it maintenance-report.service starts, waits up to ten minutes for four ports to answer — evcc on 7070, Grafana on 3000, InfluxDB on 8086, the BLE proxy on 8080 — and writes a single maintenance,phase=boot point naming what answered, what did not, and how many seconds after boot the stack was ready. InfluxDB is judged on /health returning 200 rather than on 8086 merely accepting a connection, because a cold InfluxDB opens its port well before it can answer anything. The report’s last act is to start version-logger.service, which is why the daily reading is taken by a system that has finished booting rather than one racing containers. Running the test once by hand is the only part of it that is yours — do that at the keyboard, while you are still standing next to the disk you have just plugged in.

    after sudo reboot
    findmnt /mnt/influxdb
systemctl is-active evcc grid-voltage-logger pi-throttled
docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}'
journalctl -u maintenance-report.service -b --no-pager
journalctl -u grid-voltage-logger -n 20
rfkill list
    Pass · the disk mounted from its own device as ext4, three units active, all four containers up, the boot report saying all four ports answered, the logger writing, Bluetooth unblocked and Wi-Fi still blocked.
    Three units, and only three. evcc, grid-voltage-logger and pi-throttled are the long-running services this system starts at boot; everything else it owns is a container, a timer, a one-shot, or the mount systemd generates from the /etc/fstab line. bt-unblock and maintenance-report are one-shots, so once their work is done systemctl is-active calls them inactive — which is success, not failure. That is why neither belongs on that line, and why each is proved by its own evidence instead: rfkill list for the radio, the journal for the report. version-logger.service is a one-shot too — its [Install] lives on version-logger.timer, which fires it hourly — so finding the service inactive says nothing either; it is the TIMER you ask about.
    If findmnt prints nothing and docker ps -a shows influxdb exited, read docker logs influxdb and expect a message naming /mnt/influxdb/data. That is the guard in section 13 doing exactly what it is for, and the disk is the thing to fix — journalctl -b -u mnt-influxdb.mount says why it did not mount, and lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,LABEL,MOUNTPOINTS says whether the kernel saw the disk at all. Once the mount is back, docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml up -d brings InfluxDB up again — a container that could not be created is not a container Docker’s restart policy will retry. Do not work around it by creating /mnt/influxdb/data by hand: that is the card, and InfluxDB will start on it and never tell you.

    Section 16Day-to-day operation

    On a clear day it needs nothing from you: the car starts on its own mid-morning, follows the sun, and stops when the surplus is gone. The table is what that looks like; the commands are for when you are curious.

    Want to know more?Close
    A clear summer day
    MomentWhat happens
    Early morningNothing. Surplus is below 720 W, so Solar mode holds off.
    Mid-morningSurplus passes the minimum for a full minute and the session starts, at 1–3 A.
    Around solar noonevcc modulates up to whatever the surplus supports — 3 to 6 A with the house busy. The grid tile falls to within a few tens of watts of zero, and the feed-in voltage stops climbing.
    Passing cloudCurrent drops rather than the session ending — the 10-minute disable delay rides it out.
    Late afternoonCurrent tapers with the sun. Charging continues down to 1 A.
    EveningSurplus stays below the minimum for ten minutes and the session ends. The timeline goes grey.
    Useful commands
    journalctl -u grid-voltage-logger -f       # the voltage stream, live
journalctl -u evcc -n 100 --no-pager       # recent evcc errors
docker logs -f tesla-ble-http-proxy        # traffic to the car
docker ps                                  # all four containers up
df -h /mnt/influxdb                        # the history disk, still mounted and not full
curl -s localhost:7070/api/state | jq .    # everything evcc believes
systemctl list-timers 'maintenance-*'      # when the window next fires, and when it last did
journalctl -u 'maintenance-*' -n 200       # tonight’s window so far
journalctl -u 'update-runner@*' -n 100     # every gate, in the runner’s own words
systemctl list-units 'update-runner@*'     # an update still running
sudo cat /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf   # every answer and generated secret

    Updates are no longer a button, and mostly not a decision either. The evening window does them by itself, one 22:30 timer starting the whole ordered run: the backup, then the ladder — solar-surplus first, so a new release’s pins govern the rest of the night, then evcc, grafana, influxdb, and the OS last because it is the one that can want a reboot — then the guarded reboot and the boot report on the far side of it, the whole of it finished and on the board before you are asleep. By hand it is one component at a time: sudo systemctl start update-runner@evcc.service, which is the form to reach for the first few times, because the journal shows every gate as it is passed. Exactly one thing waits for you, and it is a MAJOR version of a component whose tag is pinned in a compose file — Grafana and InfluxDB, the only two the runner has a pin to gate: the runner records approval, the board reads “Needs your yes”, and your yes is starting the raise instance — sudo systemctl start update-runner@grafana-raise.service — which proves the registry really serves the new track, writes the raised pin down where a reinstall will find it again, and takes the update in the same run. Everything else is taken without being asked about, a major of evcc or of the OS included, because they arrive through apt and there is no pin standing in front of them; that is what update by default means, and the gates that decide all of it are in section 13. The BLE proxy rides the same ladder as the rest; what is different is its pin’s shape — Docker Hub serves that image at whole x.y.z tags only, so BLE_PIN is exact and the runner moves the whole version as it takes anything below a major, while a major waits for update-runner@tesla-ble-proxy-raise.service like the other pinned two. Starting update-runner@tesla-ble-proxy.service by hand is still how you ask it what it thinks between windows, and on a healthy night the journal answers current — the check section 15 uses.

    Section 17Reference

    The tables, and the safety net: what runs on boot and what its healthy state actually looks like, what the nightly backup saves and in what order a restore brings it back — the three verbs of maintenance-backup.py, which backup.py and restore.py retired into — where every file lives and which of the two roads put it there, and the address worksheet to fill in.

    Want to know more?Close

    What runs, and what healthy looks like

    Thirteen units ship with this release, and dpkg places every one of them in /usr/lib/systemd/system/ — the vendor directory, so /etc/systemd/system stays yours to override with and nothing the release ships can collide with something you wrote. They come in three shapes, and only the first is what most people picture when they hear “service”. A daemon runs from boot to shutdown and is healthy while it reads active (running). A timer sits active (waiting) with a next elapse and does nothing else. A oneshot runs, finishes, and returns to inactive (dead) — and that is the one to read correctly, because on screen it looks exactly like a service that failed to start. It is not. It is what a finished job looks like, and systemctl status prints status=0/SUCCESS and the time it last ran directly beneath it. Judge a oneshot by its last run, never by whether it is running now.

    Units, containers and their healthy states
    UnitWhat it doesHealthy state
    evccEnergy management. evcc’s own package, not this release’s; the installer’s services step enables and starts itactive (running)
    grid-voltage-loggerThe three Smart Meter phase voltages, read from the inverter’s Solar API every 15 s and written to InfluxDB as measurement gridVoltageactive (running)
    pi-throttledThe firmware’s throttle word into bucket system every 30 s — under-voltage and thermal throttling, now and since boot. A host service, because no container reaches the firmware mailboxactive (running)
