    Files and paths — and what to back up

    These fifty-two items rebuild the system on a fresh card. Forty-six are marked custom — this release owns them — and they arrive by two roads that never cross. The deb places the code: the tree under /usr/lib/solar-surplus/ and the seventeen units in /usr/lib/systemd/system/. Then install.py renders the configuration, filling this install’s answers and freshly minted tokens into templates that ride in that same tree. The package and the configurator never write the same path, and that is the whole reason an upgrade is safe: neither can undo the other’s work, and a converge over a live system rewrites configuration without ever touching code. Two of the forty-four arrive by neither road: /etc/solar-surplus/pins and the .env beside the monitoring compose are written by the update runner on the night you raise a major, and the configurator only carries them forward. Nothing is installed to /usr/local/bin, and nothing reaches the Pi by hand. Section 13 shows the shipped files themselves.

    Files, modes and contents — files/… is /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/…, and the bare unit names are /usr/lib/systemd/system/…
    PathModeContains
    custom /usr/lib/solar-surplus/install.py755 root:rootThe configurator: seventeen steps, eight questions, every generated secret. It stays on the Pi, because every converge, every --only repair and every release upgrade starts here
    custom /usr/lib/solar-surplus/selftest.py755 root:rootThe release’s own 427 checks, read against the files beside it rather than against a description of them. get.py runs it inside a scratch copy of the deb before apt is allowed near the system, and you can run it any time: it starts no unit and makes no network call
    custom files/grid-voltage-logger.sh755 root:rootReads the three phase voltages from the Solar API every INTERVAL seconds and writes them to InfluxDB. Logic only — every address and the token come from the environment file below
    custom files/version-logger.sh755 root:rootInstalled against released for evcc, Grafana, InfluxDB, the BLE proxy and the stack itself, plus the OS’s pending-upgrade count. Sourced with VERSION_LOGGER_LIB=1 it is also the probe library the update runner re-reads versions with, so the two files can never disagree about what is installed
    custom files/update-runner.sh755 root:rootUpdates ONE component and records the outcome as one of six words. It raises a pin past a minor by itself and waits for you on a major. Logic only, no secrets
    custom files/maintenance-update.sh755 root:rootThe window’s ladder: the six runner instances started in a fixed order and waited on one at a time. It supplies order only — the serialising lock belongs to the runner, and this script must never touch it
    custom files/maintenance-reboot.sh755 root:rootThe window’s reboot, behind the maintenance lock and the runner’s lock, deferring itself if the machine booted minutes ago. Taken or deferred, the outcome is one maintenance,phase=reboot point
    custom files/maintenance-report.sh755 root:rootThe boot report: waits for evcc, Grafana, InfluxDB and the BLE proxy to answer, writes one maintenance,phase=boot point with what answered and how many seconds it took, then starts the version logger
    custom files/maintenance-window.sh755 root:rootThe whole window on demand: queues the backup, the ladder and the reboot in one systemctl run and lets the After= edges order them. Holds no lock and adds no guard — the legs guard themselves
    custom files/maintenance-clearlog.sh755 root:rootThe Clear-log press’s one act: writes the maintenance,phase=clear marker point through the grid-voltage-logger token. The Maintenance details view starts afresh at the last marker; every earlier row stays in the bucket
    custom files/window-agent.py644 root:rootThe buttons’ door: checks the token in constant time; the window route refuses while a window is running and starts maintenance-window.service, the clear route starts maintenance-clearlog.service, each through its own sudoers line. Standard library only, runs as updatesvc
    custom files/maintenance-backup.py644 root:rootBackup and restore in one file, three verbs: the nightly run, --fetch and --restore. 644 and not 755 on purpose — its unit runs python3 <path>, so nothing here needs an execute bit it could be started by accident with
    custom files/pi-throttled.sh755 root:rootReads the firmware’s throttle word (sysfs where it still exists, vcgencmd otherwise) and writes pi_throttled to bucket system — a host service, because the 6.x kernels keep the word behind the firmware mailbox, which no container reaches
    custom files/solar-surplus-dashboard.json644 root:rootSixty-eight panels, one board: the Pi’s vitals and the maintenance block down the left, every timeframed trace in a right-hand rail, the evcc content full width below. Imported through Grafana’s API at a fixed UID with overwrite, so the repo is always the board’s authority; written to the login’s home directory at 600 only if that import fails
    custom bt-unblock.service644 root:rootOne-shot rfkill unblock bluetooth, ordered before bluetooth.service
    custom grid-voltage-logger.service644 root:rootEnvironmentFile, After=docker.service evcc.service, Restart=always, and the hardening the loggers share. No RestrictAddressFamilies, on purpose: curl’s resolver needs AF_NETLINK
    custom pi-throttled.service644 root:rootThe throttle collector, cut from the same cloth — but with the default device policy left alone, because vcgencmd reaches the firmware through /dev/vchiq
    custom version-logger.service644 root:rootOne-shot, ProtectSystem=full. No [Install] section: the timer beside it carries the schedule, so it is never boot-started
    custom version-logger.timer644 root:rootOnCalendar=*-*-* *:10/15:00 — the quarter-hour version reading, at ten past and every fifteen minutes from it. Not Persistent: a Pi back from a power cut must not fire a missed reading into a stack that is still starting
    custom update-runner@.service644 root:rootTemplate, one instance per component. Not enabled — the ladder starts an instance, or you do. Nice=10 and idle I/O keep apt out of the charge loop’s way; the two-hour ceiling exists so a slow full-upgrade is never killed mid-dpkg
    custom maintenance-backup.service644 root:rootThe window’s first leg. Ninety minutes allowed, because the proven push pays for the history archive twice over the LAN. No ProtectHome — it stops and starts compose stacks under /home
    custom maintenance-window.timer644 root:rootOnCalendar=*-*-* 22:30:00, Persistent=true, no randomised delay — the evening’s one schedule, and Persistent on it means a Pi that slept through the evening takes its missed window shortly after its next boot, guards and all
    custom maintenance-update.service644 root:rootThe window’s ladder, ordered After=maintenance-backup.service — the edge that holds it behind the backup in every window
    custom maintenance-reboot.service644 root:rootThe window’s reboot, ordered after both the backup and the ladder
    custom maintenance-report.service644 root:rootThe only maintenance SERVICE with an [Install] section — both timers have theirs too, pointed at timers.target, which is how they come to be enabled at all: WantedBy=multi-user.target, so this one runs once on every boot
    custom maintenance-window.service644 root:rootThe window’s unit: oneshot, no [Install] of its own — the timer beside it carries the enablement — and a ceiling that covers the three legs’ own
    custom maintenance-clearlog.service644 root:rootThe Clear-log unit: oneshot as root over the logger’s env file, so the InfluxDB token never reaches updatesvc. No [Install] — the button starts it, blocking, and a 200 means the marker landed
    custom window-agent.service644 root:rootThe door’s unit: User=updatesvc, the field-proven hardening set with the two carve-outs sudo needs, and exit 78 excluded from restart so a bad token stops once
    custom /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger600 root:rootAddresses, org, bucket, interval and the bucket token — read by BOTH loggers, so the token is stored once. The reports, the reboot and the update runner take their InfluxDB credentials from here too
    custom /etc/default/pi-throttled600 root:rootThe throttle collector’s settings, pointed at localhost on purpose. It carries the telegraf write token, which is why it is 600
    custom /etc/default/update-runner600 root:rootNow only MONITORING_DIR and BLE_DIR, the two compose paths — absolute, because root’s ~ is /root and not yours. The charge guard and EVCC_URL are gone, with the policy that needed them
    custom /etc/default/maintenance-backup600 root:rootThe share — host, share name, account, password and the subdirectory the archives land in — the two rotation numbers, and STAGING_DIR. The password’s one copy outside install.conf and the KeePass file
    custom /etc/default/window-agent640 root:updatesvcThe board buttons’ token, the origin allow-list and the socket. Group-readable by updatesvc alone; rendered from the template and the answers, so a hand edit here is rewritten by the next converge
    custom /etc/sudoers.d/window-agent440 root:rootTWO grants: updatesvc may run systemctl start --no-block maintenance-window.service and systemctl start maintenance-clearlog.service, and nothing else. Placed by dpkg and NOT a conffile, so removing the package takes the grant with it
    custom /etc/solar-surplus/install.conf600 root:rootYour eight answers and every generated secret, in a directory at mode 700. Read on every re-run; delete a line to be asked that one question again, at a keyboard
    custom /etc/solar-surplus/pins644 root:rootOnly after you have raised one: the owner’s recorded yes to a major. An update-runner@<component>-raise run writes the track into ~/monitoring/.env first, where compose reads it, and mirrors it here second. It rides the answers archive, which is what makes a raise survive a reinstall
    custom /etc/solar-surplus/release644 root:rootOne line: the release that finished CONVERGING, not the one dpkg unpacked. Written near the end of a full run, after the last thing that can fail, and never by an --only repair; read by the version logger for the solar-surplus row — and deliberately excluded from every archive, because a restored copy would time-travel that row
    custom ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml600 USERNAMEInfluxDB 2.9 and Grafana 13.2, both pinned to a MAJOR.MINOR track through a variable a raise can move. It holds the admin credentials, which is why it is 600
    custom ~/monitoring/.env644 USERNAMEWhere compose interpolates those two pins from. A raise writes here first; install.py merges /etc/solar-surplus/pins into it on every run — merge, never overwrite: any other line in that file is yours
    custom ~/telegraf/docker-compose.yml600 USERNAMETelegraf 1.35, a literal tag rather than the movable variable pin its two neighbours carry, on the host network with / and the docker socket mounted read-only. It holds the docker group id, nothing secret; 600 for symmetry with its neighbours
    custom ~/telegraf/telegraf.conf640 USERNAME:dockerWhat Telegraf collects and where it writes: the Pi’s vitals into bucket system, 90 days. It carries the write token; group-read is what lets the container’s telegraf user open its own config
    custom ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/docker-compose.yml644 USERNAMEThe BLE proxy, network_mode: host, image pinned to 2.3.0 exactly — the only pin written down to the patch, and the reason the runner always refuses to move it for you
    custom ~/solar-surplus-secrets-v<release>.xml600 USERNAMEEvery generated secret as a KeePass 2.x import file — one entry each with URL and notes, the Samba account among them. scp it off, import it, then delete both copies
    evcc /var/lib/evcc/evcc.dbevcc's ownThe whole evcc configuration, written by the browser. Not installed and not touched by the installer; the nightly backup archives it
    ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/key/755 USERNAMEThe Charging Manager keypair. It cannot be regenerated, and losing it means re-pairing the car with the key card
    INFLUX_DIR/data/755 USERNAMEThe whole history, on the USB disk. Bound into the influxdb-data volume, not copied into it — this is the database. The largest thing here and the only thing that grows
    INFLUX_DIR/config/755 USERNAMEInfluxDB’s CLI profile, beside the data so that a disk that moves takes both
    INFLUX_DIR/backups/755 root, archives 600 USERNAMESTAGING_DIR: the nightly archives, written and proven here before they are pushed, and kept here as the tier that still works when the NAS is down. On the history disk on purpose — the next install adopts that disk untouched, which is what makes a reinstall with a surviving disk possible at all
    /var/lib/docker/volumes/monitoring_grafana-dataroot, docker’s ownThe board as Grafana holds it, on the card. It changes when you change a dashboard, not with every point logged, which is why it never needed to move to the disk
    What to back up

    Nothing, by hand. At 22:30 every night the maintenance window opens with maintenance-backup.py, which writes five archives — the answers, the pairing key, evcc’s device database, the history with every token it honours, and the board — into INFLUX_DIR/backups on the history disk, then pushes each one to your Samba share and proves the copy landed intact. Two tiers, two devices, no discipline required of you. The one thing worth checking is that both tiers are actually filling: the archives on the share should wear tonight’s date, and the board’s “Maintenance details” table says so in a row.

    Five families, and the first is the one most home-made backups are missing. answers carries /etc/solar-surplus — a few kilobytes that are the install’s identity, every password and every token. key carries ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/key/, the pairing, and is the one item here that cannot be regenerated from anything at all. evcc-db carries /var/lib/evcc/evcc.db, every device you configured in the browser. influxdb carries the disk at INFLUX_DIR and, riding inside it, /etc/solar-surplus, all four /etc/default files and telegraf.conf. grafana carries the grafana-data volume off the card. The secrets travel with the history rather than beside it because a restore that brings back the data but not its tokens produces a Pi whose loggers write to an InfluxDB that has never heard of them — and tokens without their history match nothing. They arrive together or neither is any use. The single deliberate omission is /etc/solar-surplus/release, excluded from both archives that would otherwise carry it: that file names what is installed now, and an archive’s copy of it is the past.

    The history living on its own disk changes what a backup is for. A dead card no longer takes the history with it — the disk survives, and the installer adopts it back by its label. What the archives still cover is the disk itself dying, a filesystem that will not mount, and the ordinary mistake. Two devices that fail independently is the whole benefit; treating the second one as a backup of the first is how people lose both. That is also why the staging tier sits on the disk and the pushed tier sits on the NAS, and why rotation keeps fourteen of each small family but only four of the history: identity and boards are cheap to keep for a month, and a multi-gigabyte archive is not.

    Backup, out of turnssh, or the terminal in WinSCP
    # exactly what 22:30 does, started by hand — before you change something
sudo systemctl start maintenance-backup.service
journalctl -u maintenance-backup.service -n 60 --no-pager

    What that one line does, in the order it does it. It takes /run/lock/maintenance.lock and holds it for the whole run, which is what the ladder and the reboot leg wait on, so nothing else in the window can start underneath it. It adds up what the five components occupy and refuses to begin if the staging directory has less free than that — gzip will shrink them, but a backup that gambles on the compression ratio is not a backup. It stops evcc, both loggers and both container stacks before reading a byte, because evcc.db and InfluxDB’s bolt file are live stores and a copy taken mid-write is a copy of a torn file. Each archive is written to a .partial name, read back whole with tar -tzf so gzip’s CRC and tar’s structure both have to agree, sha256-hashed with the digest printed, and only then renamed — a file that failed any of that never gets to wear a backup’s name. Everything is started again in a finally, so a failure part-way still leaves you a running system. Then each archive is pushed over smbclient and immediately fetched back to a scratch file and compared by hash: a mismatch stops the run there and rotates nothing, because a push that cannot be proved must not be allowed to retire the copy it was meant to replace. Finally both tiers are rotated to the same numbers, and one maintenance,phase=backup point is written, so the proof you just read in the terminal is also on the board.

    Two design choices in there are worth naming. The share is reached over smbclient and deliberately not mounted: a mount is one more /etc/fstab entry that can hang a boot, and this system rebooting cleanly every night is the whole point of the window. And the share password never rides on a command line — /proc shows every argv to every local process — so each run writes a private mode-600 credentials file and hands smbclient its path with -A, then deletes it. The archives exist at all because nothing here can be pulled directly with WinSCP: Grafana’s volume lives under /var/lib/docker/volumes/, the state files are root-owned, and the disk belongs to itself rather than to your home directory. An SFTP session logged in as you can see none of them, so the Pi packs what root can read into archives that anything can carry.

    Restore

    One thing about a restore matters more than everything else in this section: the answers go back before install.py, and everything else goes back after it. The answers archive is the install’s identity — every password and every token the running InfluxDB was built with. Put it back first and the installer reads it, generates nothing new, and continues that identity; the surviving database accepts this run’s tokens because they are its tokens. Run the installer first and it mints a fresh set, and then the token step meets a database that has never heard of them and stops with a 401 — correctly, but with a rebuild to unpick. Everything else has the opposite requirement: the installer is what creates the stacks, the units and the directories those archives unpack into, so they can only go back afterwards. That single ordering rule is the whole of the sequence below.

    Restore, in the one order that worksssh, on the fresh card
    # 1. the archives off the surviving disk — read-only, and unmounted again,
#    because the installer's storage step must find the disk UNmounted
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/influxdb
sudo mount -o ro /dev/disk/by-label/influxdb /mnt/influxdb
cp /mnt/influxdb/backups/*-backup-*.tar.gz /tmp/
sudo umount /mnt/influxdb

# 2. the identity, BEFORE the installer. The one rung that cannot use the
#    script, because the deb that carries the script is not on the box yet
sudo tar -xzf /tmp/answers-backup-<date>.tar.gz -C / \
     --exclude etc/solar-surplus/release etc/solar-surplus

# 3. the install — it reads those answers and continues the identity
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/mihai-gafiteanu/solar-surplus-releases/releases/latest/download/get.py
sudo python3 get.py
sudo reboot                                # the docker group

# 4. everything else, AFTER the install and its reboot
sudo python3 /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/maintenance-backup.py --restore /tmp
sudo reboot

    Step 2 is a hand-run tar rather than a verb of the script for one plain reason: on a fresh card the script does not exist yet. It arrives with the deb, and the deb arrives with get.py, which runs the installer in the same breath. So the answers rung is the one the restore verb cannot wrap — and the exclusion on that line is not decoration: a restored /etc/solar-surplus/release would tell the fresh install that this release had already converged, and it would refuse its own converge. Once the tree is on the box, --restore answers does the same thing with the same exclusion. If the disk died too and the archives are only on the NAS, copy them off the share from another machine before step 2; --fetch /tmp can only work after step 3, since the share’s settings live in a file the installer renders.

    What step 4 hides: it refuses to run if the compose stacks are missing, because it restores onto a fresh install rather than replacing one; it takes every service and both stacks down, not merely stopped, so the volumes are closed and released; it unpacks the secrets under /etc before anything starts, because every service reads them at start; it unpacks each archive to the root it was written from; it returns ownership of the key and the two disk directories to your login, since tar ran as root; it merges any raised pins back into ~/monitoring/.env, so nothing starts a default-pin container over data a raised pin wrote; it brings everything up and waits for InfluxDB, Grafana and the BLE proxy to answer; and it prints the one request that proves the pairing survived. The reboot at the end is not politeness: every unit is still holding what it read at boot, and the restore has just replaced that on disk.

    A surviving disk needs no restoring — and the restore knows

    When the card died and the disk did not, the disk is carrying the history the card lost. The installer’s storage step adopts it by its influxdb label — mounted, recorded in /etc/fstab by UUID, untouched — which is why step 1 above unmounts it again before the installer runs. --restore then skips the data inside the influxdb archive on its own and says so out loud: the mounted disk’s copy is newer than any archive’s. The secrets in that same archive are restored either way, which is the point. Only if the disk itself is what died do you want the archive’s copy, and then you say so by name — sudo python3 /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/maintenance-backup.py --restore influxdb. Even then nothing is erased: what was there is renamed to data.pre-restore-<date> beside it and left for you to delete once the board shows the restored history.

    The failure this ordering exists to prevent has a recognisable shape, so learn it once. An adopted disk holds a database built with the old secrets. If the installer ran before the answers came back it minted new ones, and the token step meets a 401: the admin token in install.conf does not match the running instance. At a terminal it will offer, at that point, to erase the history and start fresh. If you are ever offered that during a restore, stop. It means step 2 did not take. The road back is to put the answers archive in place and converge once — sudo python3 /usr/lib/solar-surplus/install.py --force — after which every generated file re-derives from the restored answers and every token matches the database it is pointed at.

    Measured, on cards rebuilt from nothing

    Measured on an early build, when the history was still a Docker volume on the card: fresh Raspberry Pi OS write, the release unpacked, installer run, archive restored, reboot — under thirty minutes end to end, and the board came back whole: the same history in the same panels, the same session totals, evcc still holding every device it was configured with, and all five components reading as up to date. Nothing was reconfigured and nothing was typed in twice.

    Measured again on 15 August 2026, on this release’s ancestor: fresh card, installer, reboot, and the pairing key alone put back by hand — the exact sequence maintenance-backup.py --restore key now runs — and the car’s body controller answered the first request. The pairing survived the reinstall with no ceremony, which was the whole claim.

    The key alone is a complete restore of the pairing

    Everything else in the archives is convenience — answers you could retype, dashboards you could rebuild, history you could live without. TeslaBleHttpProxy/key/ is different in kind: the car holds the public half, and only the key-card ceremony in section 10 can enroll a new one. Restoring that directory is the pairing. On a machine where only the key matters, name it and nothing else — sudo python3 /usr/lib/solar-surplus/files/maintenance-backup.py --restore /tmp key — and the run restores what you asked for and leaves the rest alone. The proof, with the real VIN: curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/1/vehicles/YOUR_VIN/body_controller_state" — a JSON answer means the key that came back is the one the car knows; “your public key has not been paired” means it is not, and section 10’s ceremony is the road back. The restore prints that request for you whenever the key was among the archives it put back.

    The installer’s ble step recognises a pre-existing key/ and says so, which means the order also works the other way around: put the key back before running the installer and the run itself reports the pairing as already done.

    What the script does, spelled outthe same backup and restore, by hand
    # the nightly run, by hand — five archives, everything stopped first
sudo systemctl stop evcc grid-voltage-logger.service pi-throttled.service
docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml stop
docker compose -f ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/docker-compose.yml stop
D=$(date +%F); S=/mnt/influxdb/backups; sudo mkdir -p "$S"
sudo tar -czf "$S/answers-backup-$D.tar.gz"  -C / \
     --exclude etc/solar-surplus/release etc/solar-surplus
sudo tar -czf "$S/key-backup-$D.tar.gz"      -C "$HOME" TeslaBleHttpProxy/key
sudo tar -czf "$S/evcc-db-backup-$D.tar.gz"  -C /       var/lib/evcc/evcc.db
sudo tar -czf "$S/influxdb-backup-$D.tar.gz" \
     -C /mnt --exclude etc/solar-surplus/release --exclude influxdb/backups influxdb \
     -C /    etc/solar-surplus etc/default/grid-voltage-logger \
             etc/default/pi-throttled etc/default/update-runner \
             etc/default/maintenance-backup \
     -C "$HOME" telegraf/telegraf.conf
sudo tar -czf "$S/grafana-backup-$D.tar.gz"  -C /       var/lib/docker/volumes/monitoring_grafana-data
docker compose -f ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/docker-compose.yml start
docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml start
sudo systemctl start evcc grid-voltage-logger.service pi-throttled.service

# prove each archive is readable end to end, and note its hash
for f in "$S"/*-backup-$D.tar.gz; do sudo tar -tzf "$f" >/dev/null && sha256sum "$f"; done

# the share's settings, exactly as the unit loads them — SMB_PASSWORD
# lives in that file, which is why it is 600 root:root
set -a; . /etc/default/maintenance-backup; set +a

# push one archive and prove the copy — the password in a file, never on argv
umask 077; printf 'username=%s\npassword=%s\n' "$SMB_USER" "$SMB_PASSWORD" >/tmp/.smb-auth
smbclient "//$SMB_HOST/$SMB_SHARE" -A /tmp/.smb-auth \
  -c "cd \"$SMB_DIR\"; put \"$S/key-backup-$D.tar.gz\" \"key-backup-$D.tar.gz\""
smbclient "//$SMB_HOST/$SMB_SHARE" -A /tmp/.smb-auth \
  -c "cd \"$SMB_DIR\"; get \"key-backup-$D.tar.gz\" \"$S/.check\""
sha256sum "$S/key-backup-$D.tar.gz" "$S/.check"   # the two must match
rm -f "$S/.check" /tmp/.smb-auth

# --restore, by hand — after install.py and its reboot, archives in /tmp
cd /tmp
sudo systemctl stop evcc grid-voltage-logger.service pi-throttled.service
docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml down
docker compose -f ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/docker-compose.yml down
sudo tar -xzf answers-backup-*.tar.gz  -C / --exclude etc/solar-surplus/release etc/solar-surplus
sudo tar -xzf influxdb-backup-*.tar.gz -C / --exclude etc/solar-surplus/release etc
sudo tar -xzf influxdb-backup-*.tar.gz -C "$HOME" telegraf
sudo mv /mnt/influxdb/data /mnt/influxdb/data.pre-restore-$(date +%F)  # only if the disk died
sudo tar -xzf influxdb-backup-*.tar.gz -C /mnt influxdb                # only if the disk died
sudo tar -xzf evcc-db-backup-*.tar.gz  -C /       var/lib/evcc/evcc.db
sudo tar -xzf grafana-backup-*.tar.gz  -C /       var
sudo tar -xzf key-backup-*.tar.gz      -C "$HOME" TeslaBleHttpProxy/key
sudo chown -R "$USER:$USER" ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/key /mnt/influxdb/data /mnt/influxdb/config
docker compose -f ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml up -d
docker compose -f ~/TeslaBleHttpProxy/docker-compose.yml up -d
sudo systemctl start evcc grid-voltage-logger.service pi-throttled.service
sudo reboot

    Why each line is where it is. The archives are written to /mnt/influxdb/backups and not to your home directory, because that directory is on the disk that survives a card reflash. The influxdb tar changes root three times in one command — the disk, then / for the secrets, then your home for telegraf.conf — because the secrets and the database they open must be one archive that cannot be half-restored; the two --excludes keep the release marker out and stop the archive from swallowing the directory it is being written into. On the way back, the stacks go down rather than stop, because down releases the volumes the archives are about to replace; the secrets under /etc unpack before anything starts because every service reads them at start; the archives are named from /tmp by explicit path because ~ on a fresh card is a different home than the one they were written from; the chown exists because tar ran as root; and the reboot is what turns “the files are back” into “the system read them”. What this by-hand form does not reproduce is the whole reason to let the script do it: on the way out it takes the maintenance lock so the window’s ladder cannot start underneath it, it checks there is room before it begins, it rotates both tiers to KEEP_SMALL and KEEP_INFLUX, and it writes the outcome point that puts tonight’s backup on the board; on the way back it merges any raised pins into ~/monitoring/.env before it starts a container, and waits for InfluxDB, Grafana and the BLE proxy to answer before it calls the restore done.

    Address worksheet

    Fill in the right-hand column and this becomes a map of your own system. The installer asks eight questions: the login name, two addresses, where the history disk is mounted, and the four answers that describe the Samba share the nightly backup pushes to. ROUTER_IP and CHARGER_IP are yours to look up — the installer never asks for them, but evcc and your router do. Everything below the rule is made on the machine and never printed: six secrets generated at the start of the run, three bucket-scoped tokens minted by the steps that need them, and all of them written once into ~/solar-surplus-secrets-v<release>.xml for KeePass to import.

    Placeholders and where they appear
    PlaceholderYour valueWhere it appears
    INVERTER_IP Both evcc meters, the voltage logger, the verification commands. Ports 502 (Modbus TCP) and 80 (Solar API). Asked
    PI_IP The loggers’ InfluxDB URL in /etc/default/grid-voltage-logger, every URL in the KeePass file, and the links the run prints at the end. Ports 7070 evcc · 8080 BLE proxy · 8086 InfluxDB · 3000 Grafana — the same four the boot report waits on — and 9101, the window listener. Asked
    CHARGER_IP The Wall Connector. Port 80, /api/1/vitals — typed into evcc in the browser, never into the installer
    ROUTER_IP DHCP reservations for the three devices above. Port 8443, admin
    USERNAME The SSH login, the docker group, the home the three compose stacks and the secrets file live under, and both paths in /etc/default/update-runner. Asked, defaulting to whoever ran sudo
    INFLUX_DIR Where the history disk is mounted: the two bind devices in ~/monitoring/docker-compose.yml, and INFLUX_DIR/backups, the archives’ staging tier. Asked, defaulting to /mnt/influxdb
    SMB_SERVER The server the 22:30 backup pushes to, by name or address — /etc/default/maintenance-backup. Asked
    SMB_SHARE_NAME The share on that server; the archives land in its solar-surplus subdirectory, created on the first push. Asked
    SMB_USERNAME The account the push authenticates as. Rotation deletes on the share, so it needs delete rights in its own directory. Asked
    Samba password The one question typed hidden. It lives in /etc/default/maintenance-backup and install.conf, both 600 root, and never on a command line — each run writes a private smbclient -A credentials file and deletes it afterwards
    InfluxDB instance admin tokengeneratedThe monitoring compose file, which creates the instance — and install.py on every run after that, which reads the org, the bucket and the authorisations with it, and mints and prunes the three bucket-scoped tokens below. Treat it like a root password and hand out those instead
    InfluxDB admin passwordgeneratedThe same compose file, and the browser login at port 8086
    Grafana admin passwordgeneratedThe compose file, and your login at port 3000
    Grafana viewer passwordgeneratedA read-only login for whoever checks the boards without changing them. The installer pins that account back to the Viewer role on every run
    evcc admin passwordgeneratedGenerated but not installable: evcc asks you to SET an administrator password on its first visit, and nothing here can type it in. Give it this one, and every credential of the install is in one file rather than one short of complete
    Window-button tokengeneratedThe bearer the board’s two buttons present to the window listener on 9101. It also rides, hidden, inside the dashboard, so it guards against stray LAN requests, not against anyone who can open Grafana
    InfluxDB bucket tokenmintedRead and write on evcc alone: the shared logger environment file, Grafana’s data source, and evcc’s own InfluxDB integration — the one place it still gets typed in by hand
    Telegraf write tokenmintedWrite on system alone: ~/telegraf/telegraf.conf and /etc/default/pi-throttled, the two collectors of the Pi’s own vitals
    Grafana system-bucket tokenmintedRead on system alone: the influxdb-system data source the board’s Pi half reads through

    Charging on solar surplus — build and operations documentation for a Fronius GEN24 · Tesla Wall Connector Gen 3 · Raspberry Pi 4 installation running evcc.

    Released as a Debian package, one tagged release at a time: install.py, selftest.py and the files in files/ under /usr/lib/solar-surplus/, with the fourteen units beside them. This copy of the document was last revised 2026-08-23, describing release v2.41; the download links below always serve the newest release regardless. get.py fetches it, proves its hash, and runs its self-test before anything is installed.

    Addresses appear as placeholders throughout. The installer asks for the two it needs once and substitutes them everywhere; nothing published here carries a secret.
